God promises to gather a remnant one from a city and two from a family, to give shepherds after his own heart, to make the ark unnecessary, to make Jerusalem his throne with all nations gathered, and to reunite Israel and Judah (vv. 14-18). He speaks of how he longed to be called Father (vv. 19-20). Weeping is heard on the hills, God promises I will heal your faithlessness, and the people confess their sin from their youth until now (vv. 21-25).
3.theology:
The invitation to return goes beyond what the law allows (v. 1; Deut 24:1-4): grace opens a door justice had shut, at a cost only the cross explains. Religious language and partial reform are not repentance (vv. 4-5, 10).

Greater light brings greater accountability: Judah, who watched Israel's judgment, is more guilty than Israel (v. 11). The one condition of return is honest acknowledgement of guilt (v. 13; Joel 2:12-13; 1 John 1:9).

God gathers a remnant individually (v. 14), gives shepherds after his own heart (v. 15; Acts 13:22; Eph 4:11), and will make the ark unnecessary because the presence it signified has come (vv. 16-17), with the nations gathered and the stubborn heart changed — the new covenant of chapter 31. God promises to heal faithlessness, not merely pardon it (v. 22), and the confession of vv. 24-25 follows that promise rather than earning it.
3.examples:
A door the law bolted, opened by love.

A face that has lost the ability to blush.

Judah with a front-row seat at her sister's funeral, learning nothing.

Reform that is genuine at the top and never reaches the heart.

Revival arriving one from a city and two from a family.

A sacred box no longer missed, because the presence has come.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>"If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. If you remove your detestable things from my presence, and do not waver,<sup>2</sup>and if you swear, 'As the LORD lives,' in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory."<sup>3</sup>For thus says the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: "Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.<sup>4</sup>Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of the evil of your deeds."<sup>5</sup>Declare in Judah, and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say, "Blow the trumpet through the land; cry aloud and say, 'Assemble, and let us go into the fortified cities!'<sup>6</sup>Raise a standard toward Zion, flee for safety, stay not, for I bring disaster from the north, and great destruction.<sup>7</sup>A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations has set out; he has gone out from his place to make your land a waste; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant.<sup>8</sup>For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned back from us."<sup>9</sup>"In that day, declares the LORD, courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded."<sup>10</sup>Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life."<sup>11</sup>At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A hot wind from the bare heights in the desert toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow or cleanse,<sup>12</sup>a wind too full for this comes for me. Now it is I who speak in judgment upon them."<sup>13</sup>Behold, he comes up like clouds; his chariots like the whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles— woe to us, for we are ruined!<sup>14</sup>O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?<sup>15</sup>For a voice declares from Dan and proclaims trouble from Mount Ephraim.<sup>16</sup>Warn the nations that he is coming; announce to Jerusalem, "Besiegers come from a distant land; they shout against the cities of Judah.<sup>17</sup>Like keepers of a field are they against her all around, because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD.<sup>18</sup>Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. This is your doom, and it is bitter; it has reached your very heart."<sup>19</sup>My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly; I cannot keep silent, for I hear the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war.<sup>20</sup>Crash follows hard on crash; the whole land is laid waste. Suddenly my tents are laid waste, my curtains in a moment.<sup>21</sup>How long must I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?<sup>22</sup>"For my people are foolish; they know me not; they are stupid children; they have no understanding. They are 'wise'—in doing evil! But how to do good they know not."<sup>23</sup>I looked on the earth, and behold, it was without form and void; and to the heavens, and they had no light.<sup>24</sup>I looked on the mountains, and behold, they were quaking, and all the hills moved to and fro.<sup>25</sup>I looked, and behold, there was no man, and all the birds of the air had fled.<sup>26</sup>I looked, and behold, the fruitful land was a desert, and all its cities were laid in ruins before the LORD, before his fierce anger.<sup>27</sup>For thus says the LORD, "The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end.<sup>28</sup>"For this the earth shall mourn, and the heavens above be dark; for I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back."<sup>29</sup>At the noise of horseman and archer every city takes to flight; they enter thickets; they climb among rocks; all the cities are forsaken, and no man dwells in them.<sup>30</sup>And you, O desolate one, what do you mean that you dress in scarlet, that you adorn yourself with ornaments of gold, that you enlarge your eyes with paint? In vain you beautify yourself. I am fainting before murderers."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — If You Return, Return to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return, putting away detestable things and swearing truly, so that nations shall bless themselves in him (vv. 1-2). Then the command to Judah: Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns (v. 3), and Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, lest his wrath burn unquenched (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Real return is to a person, not to a programme, and it reaches the heart or it is not return at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. If you remove your detestable things from my presence, and do not waver, and if you swear, 'As the LORD lives,' in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory." For thus says the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: "Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns. Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of the evil of your deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"If you return, O Israel, declares the LORD, to me you should return. If you remove your detestable things from my presence, and do not waver,

Chapter 3 ended with the people saying Behold, we come to you (3:22). Chapter 4 tests it. The sentence turns on a single phrase: to me you should return. Not to religion, not to the temple, not to better behaviour. To me.

It is possible to reform a life without returning to God, and the two look alike for a while. The conditions given are concrete: remove the idols, and do not waver — no half-return, no keeping the shrine in the garden in case.

and if you swear, 'As the LORD lives,' in truth, in justice, and in righteousness, then nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory."

And look where it leads. If Israel returns honestly, nations shall bless themselves in him. That is the promise made to Abraham surfacing in a sermon about repentance. A people genuinely right with God becomes the means of blessing to everyone else. The world has more at stake in the church's repentance than it knows.

For thus says the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: "Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.

Fallow ground is land that has been left unploughed so long it has hardened over. It is not barren; it is compacted. Seed thrown on it bounces. The command is not to sow harder but to break the ground first, and that is brutal work with an iron blade. Hosea said it too: Break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD (Hos 10:12).

Many people are trying to sow good seed on hard ground: more services, more resolutions, more reading, on a heart that has not been broken up in years. And sow not among thorns: clearing what chokes the seed is part of the work, as the parable of the sower says of cares and riches.

Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts, O men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem; lest my wrath go forth like fire, and burn with none to quench it, because of the evil of your deeds."

Circumcision was the covenant sign in the flesh, and every man in Judah had it. God says it has to happen somewhere else. The mark of belonging is worthless if the heart is untouched.

Now notice a difficulty the whole Bible answers. Here the people are commanded to circumcise their own hearts. In Deuteronomy God promises, the LORD your God will circumcise your heart (Deut 30:6), and in this book he will promise to write his law on it (31:33). Both are true: God commands what only he can give, and the command is how people come to ask him for it. Paul completes it: a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter (Rom 2:29), and it is done in Christ, a circumcision made without hands (Col 2:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The Alarm from the North
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The trumpet sounds and the people are told to flee to the fortified cities, for God brings disaster from the north and a destroyer of nations (vv. 5-8). Courage will fail king, officials, priests and prophets (v. 9), and Jeremiah protests that the people were told It shall be well with you (v. 10). A scorching wind comes, not to winnow or cleanse (vv. 11-13). Still the call stands: O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved (v. 14), while the besiegers close in and Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you (vv. 15-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is announced in detail, the false comfort is exposed, and in the middle of the siege the door is still open.

verseByVerse.quote: Declare in Judah, and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say, "Blow the trumpet through the land; cry aloud and say, 'Assemble, and let us go into the fortified cities!' Raise a standard toward Zion, flee for safety, stay not, for I bring disaster from the north, and great destruction. A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations has set out; he has gone out from his place to make your land a waste; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant. For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned back from us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Declare in Judah, and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say, "Blow the trumpet through the land; cry aloud and say, 'Assemble, and let us go into the fortified cities!' Raise a standard toward Zion, flee for safety, stay not, for I bring disaster from the north, and great destruction.

The tone changes without warning. An air-raid siren goes off in the middle of a sermon. Blow the trumpet, raise the signal, run for the walled towns, do not stop to pack.

And the terrible clause in the middle of the panic: for I bring disaster from the north. The invasion is not an accident of history that God will use. He is bringing it.

A lion has gone up from his thicket, a destroyer of nations has set out; he has gone out from his place to make your land a waste; your cities will be ruins without inhabitant.

The enemy is described as a lion that has left its lair and is already on the road. Nebuchadnezzar is never named here; he is simply a destroyer of nations who has set out. The tense matters. This is not a threat about what might happen if things do not improve. It has started.

For this put on sackcloth, lament and wail, for the fierce anger of the LORD has not turned back from us."

The right response to the news is not a strategy meeting but mourning. Sackcloth, lament, wailing. There is a kind of trouble that calls for grief before it calls for plans, and a church that has lost the ability to lament will meet such trouble with activity instead.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day, declares the LORD, courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded." Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life." At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A hot wind from the bare heights in the desert toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow or cleanse, a wind too full for this comes for me. Now it is I who speak in judgment upon them." Behold, he comes up like clouds; his chariots like the whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles— woe to us, for we are ruined!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day, declares the LORD, courage shall fail both king and officials. The priests shall be appalled and the prophets astounded."

The four groups again: king, officials, priests, prophets. Not one of them will have anything to say. The prophets, in particular, will be astounded — the men who had been predicting peace will be the most surprised people in the city.

Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD, surely you have utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'It shall be well with you,' whereas the sword has reached their very life."

Jeremiah's protest is startling, and the Bible records it without softening it. He hears the message of the official prophets — It shall be well with you — and he lays the responsibility at God's door.

How should this be read? Not as Scripture teaching that God lies. God's own answer comes later in the book: he never sent those prophets, and they have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace (6:14). But there is a judicial reality here that the prophet feels: when people insist on comfortable preaching, God may let them have it, and the comfortable preaching becomes part of the judgment. The sermon you most want to hear may be the most dangerous one available.

Notice too that Jeremiah says this to God, not about him behind his back. Honest protest addressed to God is a form of faith; the psalms are full of it.

At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A hot wind from the bare heights in the desert toward the daughter of my people, not to winnow or cleanse, a wind too full for this comes for me. Now it is I who speak in judgment upon them."

A farmer wants a light breeze to winnow grain, separating wheat from chaff. What is coming is the desert wind that strips the field bare: not to winnow or cleanse. This is not corrective discipline any more. It is judgment.

Behold, he comes up like clouds; his chariots like the whirlwind; his horses are swifter than eagles— woe to us, for we are ruined!

Dust on the horizon like a storm front, chariots like a whirlwind, horses faster than eagles — and then the voice of the people themselves, the first time they see it clearly: woe to us, for we are ruined!

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you? For a voice declares from Dan and proclaims trouble from Mount Ephraim. Warn the nations that he is coming; announce to Jerusalem, "Besiegers come from a distant land; they shout against the cities of Judah. Like keepers of a field are they against her all around, because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD. Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. This is your doom, and it is bitter; it has reached your very heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved. How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?

In the middle of the siege report, an invitation. The army is on the road and God is still saying that you may be saved. Mercy runs later into the story than anyone expects.

And the diagnosis is interior again: wash your heart, and the question, how long will wicked thoughts lodge within you? The word suggests a guest who has settled in. Sins that were once visitors become residents, and the difference is how long they were allowed to stay.

For a voice declares from Dan and proclaims trouble from Mount Ephraim. Warn the nations that he is coming; announce to Jerusalem, "Besiegers come from a distant land; they shout against the cities of Judah.

Dan is the northern border; Ephraim is the hill country just above Jerusalem. The report is a relay of dispatches as the enemy moves south, and the distance is closing between sentences.

Like keepers of a field are they against her all around, because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD.

A quiet, awful image. Besieging armies ring the city the way watchmen sit around a field at harvest: patient, settled, waiting for what is inside to be ready.

Your ways and your deeds have brought this upon you. This is your doom, and it is bitter; it has reached your very heart."

The same verdict as 2:17, and it needs saying plainly, because people will do almost anything to avoid it. Not every disaster is deserved; Job exists to prevent that conclusion. But some are, and pretending otherwise makes repentance impossible. It has reached your very heart — the place the whole chapter has been pointing to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly (v. 19). Crash follows hard on crash, and the prophet asks how long he must see the standard and hear the trumpet (vv. 20-21). God answers with the reason: my people are foolish; they know me not, clever at evil and ignorant of good (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who preaches the judgment is broken by it; God's word is never delivered from a safe distance.

verseByVerse.quote: My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly; I cannot keep silent, for I hear the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war. Crash follows hard on crash; the whole land is laid waste. Suddenly my tents are laid waste, my curtains in a moment. How long must I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet? "For my people are foolish; they know me not; they are stupid children; they have no understanding. They are 'wise'—in doing evil! But how to do good they know not."
verseByVerse.commentary:
My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart! My heart is beating wildly; I cannot keep silent, for I hear the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war.

The voice changes, and this is why Jeremiah is called the weeping prophet. He is not reading a bulletin. He is doubled over. My anguish, my anguish! He can feel his own heartbeat; he cannot sit still or stay quiet.

Put this beside the message he has been given to preach. He announces the disaster, and the announcement tears him apart. There is no satisfaction in him at being proved right, no relish in the doom of people who have dismissed him for years.

That is the test of anyone who handles the severe parts of Scripture. Hell, judgment and wrath can be preached with a certain enjoyment, and when they are, something has gone badly wrong. The prophet who tells the truth about judgment should be the one most obviously wounded by it.

Crash follows hard on crash; the whole land is laid waste. Suddenly my tents are laid waste, my curtains in a moment. How long must I see the standard and hear the sound of the trumpet?

The reports come in one after another, and he calls the ruined homes my tents, my curtains. These are not other people's losses to him. And then the cry every sufferer knows: How long?

"For my people are foolish; they know me not; they are stupid children; they have no understanding. They are 'wise'—in doing evil! But how to do good they know not."

God answers the How long with a diagnosis. The problem is not intelligence; it is that they know me not. And then the bitter irony: they are experts at evil and amateurs at good. Every culture has this shape — brilliant at what harms it, helpless at what would heal it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — I Looked on the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four times he looks: the earth without form and void with no light (v. 23), mountains quaking (v. 24), no man and no birds (v. 25), the fruitful land a desert (v. 26). The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end (v. 27), for God has spoken and will not turn back (vv. 28-29). The city dresses in scarlet and paint, and her lovers seek her life (v. 30); the daughter of Zion cries like a woman in labour (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment is creation running backwards, and even there God sets a limit: not a full end.

verseByVerse.quote: I looked on the earth, and behold, it was without form and void; and to the heavens, and they had no light. I looked on the mountains, and behold, they were quaking, and all the hills moved to and fro. I looked, and behold, there was no man, and all the birds of the air had fled. I looked, and behold, the fruitful land was a desert, and all its cities were laid in ruins before the LORD, before his fierce anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I looked on the earth, and behold, it was without form and void; and to the heavens, and they had no light.

Four times Jeremiah says I looked, and what he sees is Genesis played backwards. The first phrase is quoted from the creation account: The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep (Gen 1:2). Then God said, let there be light. Here the light has gone out.

I looked on the mountains, and behold, they were quaking, and all the hills moved to and fro.

Day three of creation gave dry land; here the land itself is unsteady. The earth staggers like a drunken man, says Isaiah of the same day (Isa 24:20).

I looked, and behold, there was no man, and all the birds of the air had fled.

Days five and six are undone: the birds gone, and humanity — the crown of the creation week — simply absent. There was no man.

I looked, and behold, the fruitful land was a desert, and all its cities were laid in ruins before the LORD, before his fierce anger.

This is the most terrifying passage in the book so far, and it makes a theological point that no amount of moralising could. Sin is not a private matter between a person and God with no wider consequence. It unmakes the world. Creation itself is dragged down by it, groaning, subjected to futility and waiting to be set free from its bondage to corruption (Rom 8:20-21).

Which is why salvation in the Bible is never merely the rescue of souls out of a doomed world. It is new heavens and a new earth, and the same God who spoke the first light will speak again.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, "The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end. "For this the earth shall mourn, and the heavens above be dark; for I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back." At the noise of horseman and archer every city takes to flight; they enter thickets; they climb among rocks; all the cities are forsaken, and no man dwells in them. And you, O desolate one, what do you mean that you dress in scarlet, that you adorn yourself with ornaments of gold, that you enlarge your eyes with paint? In vain you beautify yourself. Your lovers despise you; they seek your life. For I heard a cry as of a woman in labor, anguish as of one giving birth to her first child, the cry of the daughter of Zion gasping for breath, stretching out her hands, "Woe is me! I am fainting before murderers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD, "The whole land shall be a desolation; yet I will not make a full end.

Six words that keep this book from being despair: yet I will not make a full end. They will be repeated (5:10, 18). However far the judgment goes, God draws a line beyond which it will not go, and he draws it himself. A remnant will survive, and through it the promises will run on.

Jesus says the same of the worst days: if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short (Matt 24:22).

"For this the earth shall mourn, and the heavens above be dark; for I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back."

Three verbs of settled intent: spoken, purposed, not relented. Elsewhere God does relent when people turn (18:7-8), which is exactly why this is so grave. The door in verse 14 is open, and the people are not walking through it.

At the noise of horseman and archer every city takes to flight; they enter thickets; they climb among rocks; all the cities are forsaken, and no man dwells in them.

People in the bushes and up the crags, towns standing empty. The picture of refugees is ancient and current at once.

And you, O desolate one, what do you mean that you dress in scarlet, that you adorn yourself with ornaments of gold, that you enlarge your eyes with paint? In vain you beautify yourself. Your lovers despise you; they seek your life.

And here is the saddest image of the chapter. With the army at the gates, the city is doing her make-up. Scarlet, gold, painted eyes — still trying to attract the very nations whose armies are coming. Your lovers despise you; they seek your life. The alliances she trusted have turned murderous, and she is still dressing for them.

People do this. Faced with ruin, we reach for the thing that ruined us, and go on presenting a face to a world that has no intention of saving us.

For I heard a cry as of a woman in labor, anguish as of one giving birth to her first child, the cry of the daughter of Zion gasping for breath, stretching out her hands, "Woe is me! I am fainting before murderers."

The chapter ends with the cry of a woman in her first labour: pain that cannot be postponed, and hands stretched out for help. In Scripture that image is not always the end — labour pains lead somewhere, and Paul uses the same picture for a creation in the pains of childbirth (Rom 8:22). But nothing of that comfort is offered here. The chapter closes on the cry, and leaves the reader inside it.

4.title: Break Up Your Fallow Ground
4.overview:
If Israel returns, it must be to God himself, putting away idols and swearing truly, so that the nations are blessed (vv. 1-2). Judah is told to break up hard ground rather than sow among thorns, and to circumcise their hearts (vv. 3-4).

Then the alarm: the trumpet, the flight to fortified cities, a lion and destroyer of nations coming from the north, and mourning (vv. 5-8). Courage will fail every leader, and Jeremiah protests at the message of peace the people were given (vv. 9-10). A scorching wind comes, not to winnow but to judge (vv. 11-13). Still God calls Jerusalem to wash her heart that she may be saved, even as the besiegers ring the city and her own deeds close in on her (vv. 14-18).

The prophet breaks down at what he must announce (vv. 19-21), and God names the cause: a people clever at evil who do not know him (v. 22). In four visions the creation is undone — formless earth, dark heavens, quaking mountains, no people, no birds, a desert where the fruitful land was (vv. 23-26). Yet God will not make a full end (v. 27). While the land empties, the city paints her face for lovers who seek her life, and the chapter closes on a cry like a woman in labour (vv. 28-31).
4.theology:
Repentance is return to God himself, not reform of behaviour (v. 1), and it must reach the heart: the command to circumcise the heart (v. 4) is what God elsewhere promises to do (Deut 30:6; 31:33) and does in Christ (Rom 2:29; Col 2:11).

God governs the invading army: he brings the disaster (v. 6). Comfortable preaching can itself be part of judgment (v. 10; 6:14). Mercy is still offered while judgment is arriving (v. 14), and honest protest may be addressed to God (v. 10).

Sin unmakes the world: judgment is creation running backwards (vv. 23-26; Gen 1:2; Rom 8:20-22), so salvation must include a renewed creation. And God limits his own judgment — yet I will not make a full end (v. 27; Matt 24:22).
4.examples:
Ground so hard that good seed simply bounces.

A covenant sign in the body and nothing in the heart.

The sermon you most want to hear being the most dangerous one available.

Wicked thoughts that arrive as visitors and become residents.

Besiegers sitting round a city like watchmen round a field.

A city doing her make-up while the army stands at the gate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Search the Streets for One Just Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, God says, and if you can find one who does justice and seeks truth, I may pardon her (v. 1). They swear by the LORD and lie (v. 2); struck, they felt no anguish and made their faces harder than rock (v. 3). Jeremiah supposes only the poor are ignorant, but the great had broken the yoke too (vv. 4-5). So the lion, the wolf and the leopard wait (v. 6). How can I pardon you?, God asks of a people fed to the full and lusting after their neighbours' wives (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: God offers to spare a whole city for one just man, and the search fails.

verseByVerse.quote: Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, look and take note! Search her squares to see if you can find a man, one who does justice and seeks truth, that I may pardon her. Though they say, "As the LORD lives," yet they swear falsely. O LORD, do not your eyes look for truth? You have struck them down, but they felt no anguish; you have consumed them, but they refused to take correction. They have made their faces harder than rock; they have refused to repent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Run to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, look and take note! Search her squares to see if you can find a man, one who does justice and seeks truth, that I may pardon her.

God sends Jeremiah on an errand through the capital with a lamp, and the terms are extraordinary. Find one man — one — who does justice and seeks truth, and the whole city will be pardoned.

Abraham once bargained God down over Sodom, from fifty righteous to ten: For the sake of ten I will not destroy it (Gen 18:32). Here God does not wait to be bargained with. He starts at one, and he offers it about his own city, which has the temple in it, and priests in service, and a king of David's line on the throne.

The search fails. Ezekiel was given the same errand with the same result: I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none (Ezek 22:30). And the psalm had already said why: They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one (Ps 14:3).

Hold on to the shape of this verse, because the gospel is built on it. God is willing to spare a city for the sake of one righteous man. There was no such man in Jerusalem. So God provided one — and he did not spare him. Because the one just man was not spared, the city of God is.

Though they say, "As the LORD lives," yet they swear falsely.

The name of God is still in every mouth. Religious language survives long after religion has died. Using God's name to guarantee a lie is not the opposite of the problem; it is the problem.

O LORD, do not your eyes look for truth? You have struck them down, but they felt no anguish; you have consumed them, but they refused to take correction. They have made their faces harder than rock; they have refused to repent.

Three refusals, and the middle one is the most frightening: struck, and they felt no anguish. Pain is a mercy when it makes us stop. What is described here is a people who took the blows and felt nothing, whose faces have gone harder than rock. Hardness is not caused by one great sin; it is built by many small refusals.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "These are only the poor; they have no sense; for they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God. I will go to the great and will speak to them, for they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God." But they all alike had broken the yoke; they had burst the bonds. Therefore a lion from the forest shall strike them down; a wolf from the desert shall devastate them. A leopard is watching their cities; everyone who goes out of them shall be torn in pieces, because their transgressions are many, their apostasies are great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I said, "These are only the poor; they have no sense; for they do not know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God.

Jeremiah tries to rescue his own people with an explanation, and it is a very modern one. The problem is education and circumstance. These are the poor; nobody taught them. Give them better instruction and the picture will change.

I will go to the great and will speak to them, for they know the way of the LORD, the justice of their God." But they all alike had broken the yoke; they had burst the bonds.

So he goes uptown, to the educated and the powerful, who have had every advantage — and finds exactly the same thing. They all alike had broken the yoke.

That sentence dismantles a comfortable theory. Sin is not a poverty problem or an education problem. It is not solved by moving up the social scale, and the well-taught are not less guilty but more. Anyone who has worked in both kinds of community knows the truth of this: the sins differ in style and are identical in substance.

Therefore a lion from the forest shall strike them down; a wolf from the desert shall devastate them. A leopard is watching their cities; everyone who goes out of them shall be torn in pieces, because their transgressions are many, their apostasies are great.

Three predators, and the leopard is the worst image: not hunting, watching, waiting by the gate for whoever steps outside. Judgment is pictured as patient.

verseByVerse.quote: "How can I pardon you? Your children have forsaken me and have sworn by those who are no gods. When I fed them to the full, they committed adultery and trooped to the houses of whores. They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing for his neighbor's wife. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD; and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"How can I pardon you? Your children have forsaken me and have sworn by those who are no gods. When I fed them to the full, they committed adultery and trooped to the houses of whores.

How can I pardon you? is not a rhetorical shrug. It is the question of a judge who wants to acquit and cannot find grounds. God is not looking for an excuse to condemn; he is looking for a way to forgive, and the chapter has just shown that the way is not in them.

And notice the sequence: When I fed them to the full, they committed adultery. The generosity came first, and the betrayal was fuelled by it. Full stomachs and idle afternoons have ruined more people than hunger ever did.

They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing for his neighbor's wife.

The image is coarse on purpose. Men with time, money and appetite, behaving like animals in a field, and the object is specifically his neighbor's wife — the woman down the street, whose husband they know. Sin here is not abstract; it has an address.

Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD; and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?

The question will be asked again word for word in verse 29. It deserves an honest answer. A God who looked at predatory men, betrayed marriages and abandoned children and did nothing would not be loving; he would be indifferent. Wrath is not the opposite of love. Indifference is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The vine is stripped but not destroyed: make not a full end (vv. 10-11). The people say of God, He will do nothing; no disaster will come upon us, and dismiss the prophets as wind (vv. 12-13). So God makes his words in Jeremiah's mouth a fire and the people wood (v. 14), and brings a nation from afar whose language they do not know, to eat up harvest, children, flocks and fortified cities (vv. 15-17). Even then, I will not make a full end of you (v. 18), and the exile is explained: as you served foreign gods in your land, so you will serve foreigners in a land not yours (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Practical atheism — God will do nothing — is answered by a judgment shaped exactly like the sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "Go up through her vine rows and destroy, but make not a full end; strip away her branches, for they are not the LORD's. For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly treacherous to me, declares the LORD. They have spoken falsely of the LORD and have said, 'He will do nothing; no disaster will come upon us, nor shall we see sword or famine. The prophets will become wind; the word is not in them. Thus shall it be done to them!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Go up through her vine rows and destroy, but make not a full end; strip away her branches, for they are not the LORD's.

The vineyard of chapter 2 is pruned savagely — and the invaders, who think they are looting, are being given limits they know nothing about: make not a full end. Even the destruction is on a leash.

For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have been utterly treacherous to me, declares the LORD. They have spoken falsely of the LORD and have said, 'He will do nothing; no disaster will come upon us, nor shall we see sword or famine.

Here is the creed of Judah, and it is the creed of most people who have never formally denied anything: He will do nothing. Not, there is no God. Simply that he is not going to act, so his opinion need not affect any decision. It is atheism with the religion left on.

Ask what difference it would make to tomorrow if that sentence were true. For many of us the honest answer is very little, and that is the measure of how far this chapter reaches.

The prophets will become wind; the word is not in them. Thus shall it be done to them!'"

And the men who say this have a theory about preachers: they are wind, air, noise. Jeremiah heard this about himself for forty years. The insult contains its own answer, which comes in the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of hosts: "Because you have spoken this word, behold, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them. Behold, I am bringing against you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, declares the LORD. It is an enduring nation; it is an ancient nation, a nation whose language you do not know, nor can you understand what they say. Their quiver is like an open tomb; they are all mighty warriors. They shall eat up your harvest and your food; they shall eat up your sons and your daughters; they shall eat up your flocks and your herds; they shall eat up your vines and your fig trees; your fortified cities in which you trust they shall beat down with the sword." "But even in those days, declares the LORD, I will not make a full end of you. And when your people say, 'Why has the LORD our God done all these things to us?' you shall say to them, 'As you have forsaken me and served foreign gods in your land, so you shall serve foreigners in a land that is not yours.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the LORD, the God of hosts: "Because you have spoken this word, behold, I am making my words in your mouth a fire, and this people wood, and the fire shall consume them.

They called his words wind. God calls them fire. Later Jeremiah will say the word is a burning fire shut up in my bones when he tries not to speak it (20:9), and God will ask, is not my word like fire, and like a hammer that breaks rocks in pieces (23:29).

The word of God is not inert. It does something wherever it lands. A congregation that treats preaching as background noise is not thereby safe from it.

Behold, I am bringing against you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, declares the LORD. It is an enduring nation; it is an ancient nation, a nation whose language you do not know, nor can you understand what they say.

The detail that would frighten an ancient city most: you will not be able to talk to them. No negotiation, no pleading, no diplomacy — soldiers in your streets whose orders you cannot understand.

Their quiver is like an open tomb; they are all mighty warriors. They shall eat up your harvest and your food; they shall eat up your sons and your daughters; they shall eat up your flocks and your herds; they shall eat up your vines and your fig trees; your fortified cities in which you trust they shall beat down with the sword."

Four times they shall eat up, and the list moves from food to children to livelihood to defences. Everything a family works for, in order. And the last phrase names the real casualty: your fortified cities in which you trust. What falls is not only the wall but the thing the heart was leaning on.

"But even in those days, declares the LORD, I will not make a full end of you. And when your people say, 'Why has the LORD our God done all these things to us?' you shall say to them, 'As you have forsaken me and served foreign gods in your land, so you shall serve foreigners in a land that is not yours.'"

The limit is restated — I will not make a full end — and then God writes the catechism the exiles will need. They will ask why, and the answer is to be given plainly: the punishment has the same shape as the sin. You served foreign gods at home; now you will serve foreigners abroad. Sin is allowed to become a sentence, so that its true nature is finally visible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–31 — Eyes That Do Not See
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear this, O foolish and senseless people, who have eyes, but see not, who have ears, but hear not (v. 21). The sea keeps the boundary God set for it, but this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart (vv. 22-23), never saying Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rain (vv. 24-25). Wicked men trap their neighbours and grow rich, refusing justice to the fatherless and the needy (vv. 26-29). And the appalling thing: the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule at their direction; my people love to have it so, but what will you do when the end comes? (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: The sea obeys its limits and the people do not; and the lies they are told are the lies they want.

verseByVerse.quote: Declare this in the house of Jacob; proclaim it in Judah: "Hear this, O foolish and senseless people, who have eyes, but see not, who have ears, but hear not. Do you not fear me? declares the LORD. Do you not tremble before me? I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea, a perpetual barrier that it cannot pass; though the waves toss, they cannot prevail; though they roar, they cannot pass over it. But this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart; they have turned aside and gone away. They do not say in their hearts, 'Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rain in its season, the autumn rain and the spring rain, and keeps for us the weeks appointed for the harvest.' Your iniquities have turned these away, and your sins have kept good from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Declare this in the house of Jacob; proclaim it in Judah: "Hear this, O foolish and senseless people, who have eyes, but see not, who have ears, but hear not.

The organs work; the perception does not. This is the condition Isaiah was sent to describe and Jesus applied to his own generation: people who look straight at the evidence and see nothing. It is not a failure of intelligence but of the will.

Do you not fear me? declares the LORD. Do you not tremble before me? I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea, a perpetual barrier that it cannot pass; though the waves toss, they cannot prevail; though they roar, they cannot pass over it.

Stand on a beach and watch the Atlantic throw itself at the shore, and then notice what stops it: sand. Not granite cliffs. Grains. The sea has more power than every army in history and it turns back at a line of sand, because God drew the line.

The argument is sharp: the most violent thing in creation keeps the boundary God set, and you will not.

But this people has a stubborn and rebellious heart; they have turned aside and gone away. They do not say in their hearts, 'Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rain in its season, the autumn rain and the spring rain, and keeps for us the weeks appointed for the harvest.'

Notice what they fail to say, and where: in their hearts. Not a public statement, a private one. And notice what it is about — not doctrine in the abstract, but rain. The autumn rain to soften the ground for ploughing, the spring rain to swell the grain, the weeks kept for harvest: God's fingerprints on the ordinary year. Gratitude for weather is a better test of faith than most people expect.

Your iniquities have turned these away, and your sins have kept good from you.

Not every hardship is caused by sin, and this book will not let us say that. But some good things are absent from a life because sin has kept them out, and it takes honesty to consider whether that is the case.

verseByVerse.quote: For wicked men are found among my people; they lurk like fowlers lying in wait. They set a trap; they catch men. Like a cage full of birds, their houses are full of deceit; therefore they have become great and rich; they have grown fat and sleek. They know no bounds in deeds of evil; they judge not with justice the cause of the fatherless, to make it prosper, and they do not defend the rights of the needy. Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?" An appalling and horrible thing has happened in the land: the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule at their direction; my people love to have it so, but what will you do when the end comes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For wicked men are found among my people; they lurk like fowlers lying in wait. They set a trap; they catch men.

The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew here is uncertain, but the picture is clear enough. Bird-catchers crouch, wait and spring a net. What they catch is not birds: they catch men. This is predatory business, and it is happening among my people.

Like a cage full of birds, their houses are full of deceit; therefore they have become great and rich; they have grown fat and sleek. They know no bounds in deeds of evil; they judge not with justice the cause of the fatherless, to make it prosper, and they do not defend the rights of the needy.

Their houses are cages full of trapped birds, and that is how the wealth was made. Therefore they have become great and rich — the causal word is not accidental. Prosperity here is evidence, not blessing.

And the two groups they refuse are always the same two: the fatherless and the needy, the people with no one to take their case. God notices who cannot get a hearing, and he counts the failure to defend them as a deed of evil in its own right, not merely an omission.

Shall I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD, and shall I not avenge myself on a nation such as this?"

The question of verse 9 returns unchanged, now with the evidence assembled.

An appalling and horrible thing has happened in the land: the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule at their direction; my people love to have it so, but what will you do when the end comes?

The chapter ends with the most damning sentence in it, and the surprise is where the blame lands. The preachers lie. The clergy take their orders from the liars. And then: my people love to have it so.

The false prophets are not an occupying force. They are supplying a demand. A people who want to be told that everything is fine will always find someone to tell them, and will pay well for it. That is as true of a modern church choosing its teachers, or a person choosing what to read and listen to, as it was in Jerusalem.

And the last line is the question the whole book presses: what will you do when the end comes? Comfortable religion is judged not by how it feels now but by what it leaves you holding at the end. It is a question worth answering before the end asks it.

5.title: Search Her Squares: Find One Just Man
5.overview:
God sends Jeremiah through Jerusalem to find one man who does justice and seeks truth, promising to pardon the whole city for his sake; the search fails (vv. 1-3). The prophet supposes it is only the uneducated poor, but the great have broken the yoke as well (vv. 4-6). How can I pardon you?, God asks of a people whose fullness led to adultery (vv. 7-9).

The vine is stripped but not ended (vv. 10-11), because the people say He will do nothing and call the prophets wind (vv. 12-13). So God makes his words fire and the people wood, and brings a nation whose language they cannot understand to devour harvest, children, herds and walls (vv. 14-17). Even then he will not make a full end, and the exiles are given the reason: they served foreign gods at home and will serve foreigners abroad (vv. 18-19).

They have eyes and do not see (vv. 20-21). The sea keeps the boundary of sand that God set, but this people has a stubborn heart and never thanks him for the rain (vv. 22-25). Wicked men trap their neighbours and grow rich while the fatherless and needy go undefended (vv. 26-29). And the prophets lie, the priests follow them, and the people love it that way (vv. 30-31).
5.theology:
God offers to pardon a city for one righteous man and finds none (v. 1; Ezek 22:30; Ps 14:3) — the search the gospel answers, since the one just man God provided was not spared, so that the guilty city might be. Sin is not a matter of class or education (vv. 4-5).

God's wrath is the response of love to predation and betrayal, not the opposite of love (vv. 9, 29). His word is fire, never inert (v. 14; 23:29). Judgment is limited by God himself (vv. 10, 18) and shaped to fit the sin (v. 19).

Creation obeys the boundaries God sets and his people do not (v. 22). False teaching flourishes because people want it (v. 31), and comfortable religion is tested by what it leaves a person holding at the end.
5.examples:
A search of the whole city for one honest man, and it comes up empty.

The theory that better education would fix it, tested uptown.

"He will do nothing": atheism with the religion left on.

Soldiers in your streets whose orders you cannot understand.

The Atlantic turned back by a line of sand.

Preachers who lie, and a people who love to have it so.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The alarm sounds again: flee, blow the trumpet, raise a signal, for disaster looms out of the north (vv. 1-2). Enemy commanders pitch their tents around the city like shepherds around a pasture and plan the assault by day and by night (vv. 3-5). This is the city that must be punished; there is nothing but oppression within her (v. 6), for she keeps her evil fresh as a well keeps its water (v. 7). Still a warning stands: Be warned, O Jerusalem, lest I turn from you in disgust (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The siege is described in detail and the warning is still open: even here God says be warned, not farewell.

verseByVerse.quote: Flee for safety, O people of Benjamin, from the midst of Jerusalem! Blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and raise a signal on Beth-haccherem, for disaster looms out of the north, and great destruction. The lovely and delicately bred I will destroy, the daughter of Zion. Shepherds with their flocks shall come against her; they shall pitch their tents around her; they shall pasture, each in his place. "Prepare war against her; arise, and let us attack at noon! Woe to us, for the day declines, for the shadows of evening lengthen! Arise, and let us attack by night and destroy her palaces!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flee for safety, O people of Benjamin, from the midst of Jerusalem! Blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and raise a signal on Beth-haccherem, for disaster looms out of the north, and great destruction.

Jeremiah was from Benjamin, and his own people are the first told to run. The signals go up on the hills south of the city: Tekoa and Beth-haccherem were beacon stations. The warning system is working perfectly, and it is carrying bad news.

The lovely and delicately bred I will destroy, the daughter of Zion.

The ESV notes another possible rendering, "I have likened the daughter of Zion to the loveliest pasture", which fits the shepherds in the next verse. Either way the point is the contrast between what she is — lovely, sheltered, brought up in comfort — and what is about to happen to her.

Shepherds with their flocks shall come against her; they shall pitch their tents around her; they shall pasture, each in his place.

A pastoral picture turned menacing. These shepherds are enemy commanders, their flocks are armies, and the city is the field they will graze bare. Each takes his own section of wall, the way a shepherd takes his own patch of grass. Sieges are patient work.

"Prepare war against her; arise, and let us attack at noon! Woe to us, for the day declines, for the shadows of evening lengthen! Arise, and let us attack by night and destroy her palaces!"

Now we hear the soldiers talking among themselves, and it is chilling because of the eagerness. Attack at midday. Frustrated that the light is going, they decide to attack at night instead. Men who cannot wait to destroy somebody's home. Every war has this voice in it, and Scripture lets us hear it.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts: "Cut down her trees; cast up a siege mound against Jerusalem. This is the city that must be punished; there is nothing but oppression within her. As a well keeps its water fresh, so she keeps fresh her evil; violence and destruction are heard within her; sickness and wounds are ever before me. Be warned, O Jerusalem, lest I turn from you in disgust, lest I make you a desolation, an uninhabited land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the LORD of hosts: "Cut down her trees; cast up a siege mound against Jerusalem. This is the city that must be punished; there is nothing but oppression within her.

The orders come from God, not from the invading general. The trees around the city are felled for the ramp — a detail any ancient reader would recognise as the beginning of the end.

And the charge is named: there is nothing but oppression within her. Not idolatry this time, but the treatment of people. In the prophets, worship and justice are never separated for long.

As a well keeps its water fresh, so she keeps fresh her evil; violence and destruction are heard within her; sickness and wounds are ever before me.

A remarkable image, and a bitter one. A good well keeps its water fresh; Jerusalem keeps her evil fresh, constantly replenished, never going stale. Whatever she is good at preserving, it is not righteousness.

And notice the last phrase: sickness and wounds are ever before me. God is not detached from what the city does to its weak. He is looking at the injuries, continuously.

Be warned, O Jerusalem, lest I turn from you in disgust, lest I make you a desolation, an uninhabited land."

After all that, a warning rather than a verdict: Be warned. The siege ramp is going up and God is still speaking as though it might be stopped. This is the pattern of the book, and it repays noticing every time, because it tells us what God is like.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — Peace, Peace, When There Is No Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The remnant will be gleaned like a vine (v. 9). To whom can Jeremiah speak? their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen, and the word of the LORD is to them an object of scorn (v. 10). He is full of the wrath of the LORD and weary of holding it in (vv. 11-12). From the least to the greatest of them, everyone is greedy for unjust gain; and from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely (v. 13), and They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace (v. 14) — and they could not blush (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: A wound treated lightly is the classic failure of false religion: comfort offered where surgery is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts: "They shall glean thoroughly as a vine the remnant of Israel; like a grape gatherer pass your hand again over its branches." To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the LORD is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it. Therefore I am full of the wrath of the LORD; I am weary of holding it in. "Pour it out upon the children in the street, and upon the gatherings of young men, also; both husband and wife shall be taken, the elderly and the very aged. Their houses shall be turned over to others, their fields and wives together, for I will stretch out my hand against the inhabitants of the land," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD of hosts: "They shall glean thoroughly as a vine the remnant of Israel; like a grape gatherer pass your hand again over its branches."

Gleaning is the second pass over a vine, the careful hand going back along branches already picked. Applied to an army it means thoroughness: the invaders will not leave much, and what the first sweep missed the second will take.

To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the LORD is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it.

The prophet's despair is practical: who is left to talk to? In chapter 4 the problem was uncircumcised hearts; here it is uncircumcised ears, sealed over, incapable of hearing. And the diagnosis ends with a phrase worth pausing on: they take no pleasure in it.

That is the deepest measure of a spiritual condition — not whether a person can argue with the Bible, but whether it gives them any pleasure. A believer's love for the word waxes and wanes, but total distaste for it is a symptom that ought to be taken seriously.

Therefore I am full of the wrath of the LORD; I am weary of holding it in. "Pour it out upon the children in the street, and upon the gatherings of young men, also; both husband and wife shall be taken, the elderly and the very aged. Their houses shall be turned over to others, their fields and wives together, for I will stretch out my hand against the inhabitants of the land," declares the LORD.

Jeremiah, who wept in chapter 4, is here full of the wrath of the LORD and tired of containing it. Both are true of him, and neither cancels the other. A man who feels only anger at a corrupt society has stopped loving it; a man who feels no anger has stopped taking its victims seriously.

The list that follows spares nobody: children, young men, married couples, the elderly. Judgment on a nation always lands on the whole household, which is one reason it is so grievous and why God delays it so long.

verseByVerse.quote: "For from the least to the greatest of them, everyone is greedy for unjust gain; and from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace. Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; at the time that I punish them, they shall be overthrown," says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For from the least to the greatest of them, everyone is greedy for unjust gain; and from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely.

Two totals: from bottom to top of society, and from prophet to priest within the church. Greed at every social level, dishonesty at every religious level. When the leadership is corrupt there is nowhere left to appeal.

They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace.

This is one of the most quoted sentences in Jeremiah, and it should be, because it describes a permanent temptation. The wound is real. The treatment is a clean bandage over an infected cut and a reassuring word: Peace, peace.

Why would anyone do that? Because it is what the patient wants, because the true diagnosis is unbearable to deliver, and because the healer gets thanked for it in the short term. Micah heard the same men: yet they lean on the LORD and say, "Is not the LORD in the midst of us? No disaster shall come upon us" (Mic 3:11).

The test for any preaching, counselling or friendship is whether it deals with the wound or only with the feeling about the wound. A gospel that never mentions sin is a bandage over an infection, and the kindness of it is an illusion that costs the patient everything.

Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; at the time that I punish them, they shall be overthrown," says the LORD.

They did not know how to blush. Not that they refused; they had lost the ability. Shame is a nerve ending, and a conscience can lose feeling the way a limb does. The loss is quiet and is usually mistaken for maturity or confidence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — Ask for the Ancient Paths
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it' (v. 16). Watchmen were set and ignored (v. 17). So the nations are called to witness the disaster coming, the fruit of their devices (vv. 18-19). Frankincense from Sheba is no use; their offerings are not acceptable (v. 20), and stumbling blocks are laid in their path (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The old way is not nostalgia but the road that leads home, and refusing it is a decision, not an accident.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it.' I set watchmen over you, saying, 'Pay attention to the sound of the trumpet!' But they said, 'We will not pay attention.' Therefore hear, O nations, and know, O congregation, what will happen to them. Hear, O earth; behold, I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words; and as for my law, they have rejected it. What use to me is frankincense that comes from Sheba, or sweet cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices pleasing to me. Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will lay before this people stumbling blocks against which they shall stumble; fathers and sons together, neighbor and friend shall perish.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it.'

Four imperatives, and they are the cure for everything this chapter has described. Stand — stop moving long enough to think. Look — consider the roads in front of you. Ask — for the old paths, which means asking someone who knows them. Walk — the point of the whole exercise, because knowing the way home and standing at the junction is not the same as going.

This is not nostalgia for an older decade. The ancient paths are the ways God gave, which are older than the fashion of any era and do not need replacing every generation. The promise attached is not success but rest: find rest for your souls.

Jesus takes that exact phrase and offers it in his own name: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls (Matt 11:29). The ancient path, it turns out, is a person.

And then the refusal, in five flat words: We will not walk in it. Not a failure of information. A decision.

I set watchmen over you, saying, 'Pay attention to the sound of the trumpet!' But they said, 'We will not pay attention.'

The same shape again: God provides, they refuse. The watchmen are the prophets, whose job was to see trouble early and shout. The refusal here is not of a burden but of an alarm, which is a strange thing to resent until you remember what alarms interrupt.

Therefore hear, O nations, and know, O congregation, what will happen to them. Hear, O earth; behold, I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words; and as for my law, they have rejected it.

The nations are called as witnesses, and the sentence is described as the fruit of their devices: what grew from the seed they planted. God's judgment is often the ripening of what people have themselves sown.

What use to me is frankincense that comes from Sheba, or sweet cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, nor your sacrifices pleasing to me.

Expensive imported incense, the best available, and God says it is no use to him. The prophets say this repeatedly — I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams (Isa 1:11); I hate, I despise your feasts (Amos 5:21); I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hos 6:6) — and it is never an attack on worship as such. It is the refusal to accept worship as a substitute for obedience. Generous giving and faithful attendance can both be ways of buying God off.

Therefore thus says the LORD: 'Behold, I will lay before this people stumbling blocks against which they shall stumble; fathers and sons together, neighbor and friend shall perish.'"

The road they refused to walk becomes a road they cannot walk. Refused grace hardens into obstacles, and whole families and friendships go down together.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A cruel people comes from the north, the sound of them is like the roaring sea (vv. 22-23). Hands fall helpless; terror is on every side (vv. 24-25); mourning is to be as for an only son (v. 26). Jeremiah is made a tester of metals among his people (v. 27), but they are bronze and iron, and in vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed (vv. 28-29). Rejected silver they are called, for the LORD has rejected them (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology: The assay is run honestly and the metal fails; only a better refining, and a better price, can save such people.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Behold, a people is coming from the north country, a great nation is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth. They lay hold on bow and javelin; they are cruel and have no mercy; the sound of them is like the roaring sea; they ride on horses, set in array as a man for battle, against you, O daughter of Zion!" We have heard the report of it; our hands fall helpless; anguish has taken hold of us, pain as of a woman in labor. Go not out into the field, nor walk on the road, for the enemy has a sword; terror is on every side. O daughter of my people, put on sackcloth, and roll in ashes; make mourning as for an only son, most bitter lamentation, for suddenly the destroyer will come upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD: "Behold, a people is coming from the north country, a great nation is stirring from the farthest parts of the earth. They lay hold on bow and javelin; they are cruel and have no mercy; the sound of them is like the roaring sea; they ride on horses, set in array as a man for battle, against you, O daughter of Zion!"

Sound before sight: an army heard before it is seen, like surf. Cruel and have no mercy is not propaganda; it is the plain character of ancient warfare, and God is telling his people the truth about what is coming rather than letting them imagine a manageable version.

We have heard the report of it; our hands fall helpless; anguish has taken hold of us, pain as of a woman in labor.

The people answer, and for the first time they are not arguing. Our hands fall helpless. The bravado of chapter 5 is gone. It took the sound of the sea to produce it.

Go not out into the field, nor walk on the road, for the enemy has a sword; terror is on every side.

Terror is on every side becomes a refrain in this book, and later it will be turned into a nickname thrown at Jeremiah himself (20:10). Here it is simply life under siege: the ordinary movements of a working day — going to the field, walking the road — become impossible.

O daughter of my people, put on sackcloth, and roll in ashes; make mourning as for an only son, most bitter lamentation, for suddenly the destroyer will come upon us.

The deepest grief the ancient world could name was the loss of an only son: the end of a family line and every hope with it. That is the measure of mourning God prescribes here, and it is the grief that God himself will one day undergo for these people.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have made you a tester of metals among my people, that you may know and test their ways. They are all stubbornly rebellious, going about with slanders; they are bronze and iron; all of them act corruptly. The bellows blow fiercely; the lead is consumed by the fire; in vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed. Rejected silver they are called, for the LORD has rejected them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I have made you a tester of metals among my people, that you may know and test their ways.

A new picture for the prophet's work. He is an assayer: the man who takes a sample, heats it, and reports what the metal actually is. Preaching tests people. The same word that softens one heart hardens another, and the reaction is the assay.

They are all stubbornly rebellious, going about with slanders; they are bronze and iron; all of them act corruptly.

The sample comes back as base metal. Bronze and iron are useful and they are not silver, which is what this refining was meant to produce.

The bellows blow fiercely; the lead is consumed by the fire; in vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed.

Refiners used lead to draw impurities out of silver. Here the process is run to the limit: the bellows roar, the lead burns away, and nothing pure emerges. In vain the refining goes on.

The fire in this image is the long series of national disasters God has already sent — the invasions, the droughts, the warnings. Suffering refines some people and hardens others, and the difference is not in the furnace.

Rejected silver they are called, for the LORD has rejected them."

The chapter ends with the assayer's certificate, and it is a verdict of worthlessness: metal that failed the test, put aside. It is among the bleakest endings in the book.

And it is exactly why the New Testament's language about redemption lands with such force. Peter tells Christians they were ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet 1:18-19). Rejected silver cannot buy anything. But rejected people can be bought back, by a price that does not come from the furnace at all.

6.title: Peace, Peace, When There Is No Peace
6.overview:
The alarm sounds again from the hills: disaster is coming from the north (vv. 1-2). Enemy commanders camp around Jerusalem like shepherds around a pasture and plan their assault (vv. 3-5). God himself orders the siege ramp, because the city is full of oppression and keeps her evil fresh as a well keeps water — and still says, Be warned, O Jerusalem (vv. 6-8).

There is no one left to warn: their ears are uncircumcised and God's word gives them no pleasure (vv. 9-10). The prophet is full of God's wrath and weary of holding it in (vv. 11-12). Everyone from least to greatest is greedy, and prophets and priests deal falsely, healing the wound lightly and saying Peace, peace where there is none; they have lost the ability to blush (vv. 13-15).

God calls them to stand at the crossroads and ask for the ancient paths, where they will find rest for their souls, and they answer We will not walk in it (vv. 16-17). So disaster comes as the fruit of their own devices, and costly incense will not buy it off (vv. 18-21). A cruel nation approaches with a sound like the sea; terror is on every side; mourn as for an only son (vv. 22-26). Finally Jeremiah is made an assayer, and the metal fails the test: Rejected silver they are called (vv. 27-30).
6.theology:
God directs the armies that punish his people (v. 6), and warns even while the siege ramp rises (v. 8). Spiritual deadness shows itself as an inability to hear and a distaste for God's word (v. 10).

False ministry treats a deep wound lightly and calls it peace (v. 14; Mic 3:11); true ministry names the wound. The remedy is the old way God gave, and the rest it promises is fulfilled in Christ's invitation (v. 16; Matt 11:29). Worship offered as a substitute for obedience is rejected (v. 20; Isa 1:11; Amos 5:21; Hos 6:6).

Judgment is often the ripening of what people themselves sowed (v. 19). Suffering refines some and hardens others (vv. 27-29), and those who fail the assay are redeemed, if at all, by a price from outside the furnace (1 Pet 1:18-19).
6.examples:
Soldiers impatient at sunset because they cannot attack yet.

A well that keeps its water fresh, and a city that keeps its evil fresh.

A clean bandage over an infected wound, and a reassuring word.

A conscience that has lost feeling the way a limb does.

Standing at the junction knowing the way home, and not walking it.

An assayer's certificate that reads: rejected.
