And they pour out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me to anger.<sup>19</sup>Is it I whom they provoke? declares the LORD. Is it not themselves, to their own shame?<sup>20</sup>Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground; it will burn and not be quenched."<sup>21</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh.<sup>22</sup>For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices.<sup>23</sup>But this command I gave them: 'Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. And walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.'<sup>24</sup>But they did not obey or incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels and the stubbornness of their evil hearts, and went backward and not forward.<sup>25</sup>From the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets to them, day after day.<sup>26</sup>Yet they did not listen to me or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck. They did worse than their fathers.<sup>27</sup>"So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you. You shall call to them, but they will not answer you.<sup>28</sup>And you shall say to them, 'This is the nation that did not obey the voice of the LORD their God, and did not accept discipline; truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips.<sup>29</sup>"'Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.'<sup>30</sup>"For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, declares the LORD. They have set their detestable things in the house that is called by my name, to defile it.<sup>31</sup>And they have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind.<sup>32</sup>Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it will no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter; for they will bury in Topheth, because there is no room elsewhere.<sup>33</sup>And the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the air, and for the beasts of the earth, and none will frighten them away.<sup>34</sup>And I will silence in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, for the land shall become a waste.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah is told to stand in the gate of the temple and preach to the worshippers coming in (vv. 1-2): Amend your ways and your deeds, and I will let you dwell in this place (v. 3). Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD' (v. 4). The conditions are named: true justice, no oppression of the sojourner, the fatherless or the widow, no innocent blood, no other gods — then I will let you dwell in this place (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: A building, however holy, guarantees nothing; God attaches his promise to repentance and to the treatment of the weak.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Stand in the gate of the LORD's house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the LORD, all you men of Judah who enter these gates to worship the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD: "Stand in the gate of the LORD's house, and proclaim there this word, and say, Hear the word of the LORD, all you men of Judah who enter these gates to worship the LORD.

The place is chosen deliberately. Not the market, not the palace: the temple gate, on a day when crowds are streaming in to worship. Jeremiah is to stand where the traffic is thickest and preach to religious people on their way to a service.

That is a harder assignment than preaching to pagans. Everyone coming through those gates believes they are doing the right thing, and they are — the worship is commanded, the temple is God's own house. The problem is not that they are absent from church.

This sermon is told again in chapter 26, where we learn what it cost: priests and prophets seized him and said, You shall die! Nothing provokes like a word against a religion people are relying on.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Amend your ways and your deeds, and I will let you dwell in this place. Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Amend your ways and your deeds, and I will let you dwell in this place.

The offer is unchanged from chapter 4: change, and stay. God is not announcing an unavoidable fate; he is naming a condition. And the condition is your ways and your deeds — conduct, not ceremony.

Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.'

Here is the sentence that made the sermon famous, and it quotes a chant. Three times, like a slogan at a rally: the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD. It was their confidence. God lives here. The ark is here. He will never let this city fall, because his own house is in it.

And God calls it deceptive words. Notice: every word of the chant was true. The building really was his temple. What made it deceptive was what they were doing with the truth — using it as a reason to feel safe while living as they pleased.

It is the easiest error in the world to repeat. A denomination, a confession, a conversion experience, a baptism, a church membership, a family heritage: all good, all true, all capable of becoming a chant that shields a person from the question of how he actually lives. Jesus finished his greatest sermon on this note — the man who hears and does not do is building on sand, and great was the fall of it (Matt 7:27).

verseByVerse.quote: "For if you truly amend your ways and your deeds, if you truly execute justice one with another, if you do not oppress the sojourner, the fatherless, or the widow, or shed innocent blood in this place, and if you do not go after other gods to your own harm, then I will let you dwell in this place, in the land that I gave of old to your fathers forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For if you truly amend your ways and your deeds, if you truly execute justice one with another, if you do not oppress the sojourner, the fatherless, or the widow, or shed innocent blood in this place, and if you do not go after other gods to your own harm, then I will let you dwell in this place, in the land that I gave of old to your fathers forever.

God spells out what amendment would look like, and the list repays a slow reading because of what is in it and what is not.

It begins with justice one with another: ordinary dealings between neighbours. Then three groups: the sojourner, the immigrant with no family network; the fatherless; the widow. In that society these three had no one to take their case and no way to enforce a claim. God names them every time, and he makes his continued presence with the nation turn on how they are treated.

Then innocent blood, and only last the matter of other gods. A modern reader expects a religious checklist. God gives a mostly social one, and does not thereby make the vertical less important — verse 6 ends with idolatry, and the sermon is being preached in his temple. But he refuses to let the two be separated. A church that is orthodox on Sunday and indifferent to the vulnerable on Monday has not passed this test; it has failed the half of it that God put first.

And notice the repeated word: truly. Twice in one sentence. There is a way of doing justice for the appearance of it, and God distinguishes it from the real thing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — As I Did to Shiloh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behold, you trust in deceptive words to no avail (v. 8). Will you break the commandments and then stand in this house and say We are delivered!, only to go on doing it (vv. 9-10)? Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? (v. 11). Go and look at Shiloh, where God's name first dwelt, and see what he did to it (v. 12); the same will be done to this house and this people (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The place God chose can be destroyed by God: Shiloh is the precedent, and the temple is not exempt.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, you trust in deceptive words to no avail. Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal, and go after other gods that you have not known, and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!'—only to go on doing all these abominations? Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I myself have seen it, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, you trust in deceptive words to no avail. Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal, and go after other gods that you have not known,

Read that list against the Ten Commandments: stealing, murder, adultery, false swearing, other gods. They are breaking the commandments one after another, and God lists them as a bill of particulars.

and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!'—only to go on doing all these abominations?

Here is the scene: from the sin straight to the service, standing in God's house saying We are delivered! and going out to do it all again. The word translated delivered is the language of rescue, and it is being used as an insurance policy.

The phrase only to go on doing all these abominations is the sting. Worship had become the thing that made the sin sustainable. Confession without any intention to stop is not repentance; it is maintenance.

Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I myself have seen it, declares the LORD.

A den is not where robbers rob. It is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they feel safe and divide the takings. That is what the temple had become: a hideout. They did their damage in the city and came here to be secure.

Six centuries later Jesus walked into the same courts, overturned the tables and quoted this verse: My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers (Matt 21:13). He was not merely objecting to commerce. He was charging that generation with Jeremiah's indictment, and, like Jeremiah, he went on to predict that the building would come down.

And the last clause removes every hiding place: Behold, I myself have seen it.

verseByVerse.quote: Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel. And now, because you have done all these things, declares the LORD, and when I spoke to you persistently you did not listen, and when I called you, you did not answer, therefore I will do to the house that is called by my name, and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh. And I will cast you out of my sight, as I cast out all your kinsmen, all the offspring of Ephraim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel.

God sends them on a field trip. Shiloh was where the tabernacle stood for generations before the temple was built; it was the first place God caused his name to dwell. In Eli's day the ark was carried out of Shiloh into battle as a talisman, and Israel was slaughtered and the ark of God was captured (1 Sam 4:11). The psalm records the end of it: He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind (Ps 78:60).

The ruins were about twenty miles north, close enough to walk to. Go and look, God says. That is what I do to a holy place that has become a charm.

And now, because you have done all these things, declares the LORD, and when I spoke to you persistently you did not listen, and when I called you, you did not answer, therefore I will do to the house that is called by my name, and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh.

The sentence is exact: the house in which you trust will go the way of Shiloh. Misplaced trust is not protected by being religious trust. If anything it is treated more severely, because it uses God's own gifts as insulation against him.

And I will cast you out of my sight, as I cast out all your kinsmen, all the offspring of Ephraim.

Ephraim is the northern kingdom, gone a century before. Judah had watched it happen (3:8) and concluded that it could not happen to them, because they had the temple. God says the precedent stands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Do Not Pray for This People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As for you, do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer for them, and do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you (v. 16). God points to what they are doing: whole families working together — children gathering wood, fathers kindling fire, women kneading dough — to make cakes for the queen of heaven (vv. 17-18). Is it I whom they provoke?, he asks; Is it not themselves, to their own shame? (v. 19). So his wrath will be poured out on man, beast and field (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The forbidding of intercession is the most solemn moment yet, and even it is framed by the fact that sin destroys the sinner first.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer for them, and do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you. Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven. And they pour out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me to anger. Is it I whom they provoke? declares the LORD. Is it not themselves, to their own shame? Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground; it will burn and not be quenched."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As for you, do not pray for this people, or lift up a cry or prayer for them, and do not intercede with me, for I will not hear you.

This is among the most frightening verses in Scripture, and it is aimed at the intercessor rather than at the guilty. Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for his own nation. The prohibition comes three times in this book (11:14; 14:11), which tells us he kept doing it anyway.

What does it mean? Not that God has stopped being merciful — the same book will promise a new covenant. It means that a point can be reached where judgment is settled and further pleading will not turn it aside; and it means God is telling his prophet in advance, so that when the city falls Jeremiah will not think his prayers failed.

John writes something in the same territory: There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that (1 John 5:16). These are not verses to wield against people we have given up on. Nobody can read another person's file. They are warnings about how serious sustained refusal is, and they are rare precisely because the normal command is to pray for everyone.

Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? The children gather wood, the fathers kindle fire, and the women knead dough, to make cakes for the queen of heaven. And they pour out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me to anger.

God shows him why. It is a family scene, and that is what makes it terrible: children collecting kindling, fathers at the fire, mothers making the dough. Everyone has a job, and the whole household is at work on idolatry. It is cosy. It is also the most efficient way to hand a religion to the next generation.

Is it I whom they provoke? declares the LORD. Is it not themselves, to their own shame?

A question that changes the temperature. God is not a deity whose dignity has been dented. The damage of sin falls first on the sinner: Is it not themselves? His anger is not wounded pride; it is the response of love to people destroying themselves and their children.

Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, my anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground; it will burn and not be quenched."

And the land itself suffers with the people, as it did in the un-creation vision of chapter 4. Human sin is never contained within the human sphere.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh (v. 21): at the exodus God's command was not first about sacrifices but Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people (vv. 22-23). They did not obey but went backward and not forward (v. 24), though God sent his prophets day after day (vv. 25-26). Jeremiah is told they will not listen to him either (v. 27), and must say, truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips (vv. 28-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Sacrifice was never meant to replace obedience, and centuries of persistent preaching have met a stiffened neck.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh. For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this command I gave them: 'Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. And walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.' But they did not obey or incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels and the stubbornness of their evil hearts, and went backward and not forward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: "Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh.

The tone is sardonic. In the burnt offering the whole animal was burned to God; in other sacrifices the worshippers ate part of the meat. God says: go ahead, put them all together and eat the lot yourselves. If the sacrifices mean nothing, they may as well be dinner.

For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this command I gave them: 'Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. And walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.'

Read carelessly, this sounds like a denial that God gave the sacrificial law, which would contradict Leviticus. Read in its own terms, it is about what came first and what it was for. At the exodus the founding word was not a manual of offerings but a relationship: Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. The sacrifices were given inside that covenant to serve it, never to replace it.

The prophets say this in one voice. To obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22). I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (Hos 6:6). Bring no more vain offerings, and instead learn to do good; seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause (Isa 1:13, 17). Let justice roll down like waters (Amos 5:24).

The modern equivalents are obvious enough: attendance, giving, service, the right doctrinal words. Every one is good. Every one can be offered instead of obedience.

But they did not obey or incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels and the stubbornness of their evil hearts, and went backward and not forward.

Backward and not forward: the whole history in three words. There is no standing still in this book. A people either walks in the way it is shown or drifts back from it.

verseByVerse.quote: From the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets to them, day after day. Yet they did not listen to me or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck. They did worse than their fathers. "So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you. You shall call to them, but they will not answer you. And you shall say to them, 'This is the nation that did not obey the voice of the LORD their God, and did not accept discipline; truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips. "'Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets to them, day after day.

Persistently, and day after day, for centuries. That is God's patience measured in messengers: not one warning ignored, but a stream of them across generations, each one a mercy.

Yet they did not listen to me or incline their ear, but stiffened their neck. They did worse than their fathers.

A stiffened neck is the animal that will not turn its head to the rein. And the last sentence removes the excuse of inheritance: They did worse than their fathers. Each generation had the added evidence of what the previous one had suffered, and went further anyway.

"So you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you. You shall call to them, but they will not answer you.

Here is a commission almost no one would accept: preach, and they will not listen; call, and no one will answer. God tells his servant the outcome in advance, and still sends him.

That reframes what faithfulness is. Jeremiah is not sent to be effective; he is sent to be faithful. Results are God's business. Anyone serving in a hard place — a stagnant church, an indifferent family, a class that does not care — is standing where Jeremiah stood, and the standard by which the work will be judged is the one given here.

And you shall say to them, 'This is the nation that did not obey the voice of the LORD their God, and did not accept discipline; truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips.

Truth has perished: not merely that people tell lies, but that truth itself has died as a public commodity, so that no one expects it in a courtroom, a market or a temple. A society can survive a great deal of wickedness; it cannot survive the death of truth, because nothing can then be repaired.

"'Cut off your hair and cast it away; raise a lamentation on the bare heights, for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.'

Cutting the hair was a public sign of grief, and the bare heights were the hills where the idolatry had been practised. Go back to the scene of the sin, God says, and hold the funeral there.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They have defiled the temple with their idols (v. 30) and built the high places of Topheth to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind (v. 31). So Topheth will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, with burials there for lack of room and bodies left for the birds (vv. 32-33). And God will silence the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: The valley where children were burned gives its name to the place of judgment, and the sound that ends is the sound of weddings.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, declares the LORD. They have set their detestable things in the house that is called by my name, to defile it. And they have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, declares the LORD. They have set their detestable things in the house that is called by my name, to defile it.

The idols are not only in the villages now; they are inside the temple. The building they chanted about had been furnished with the very things that made it uninhabitable for God.

And they have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind.

This is the floor of the book. In a ravine outside Jerusalem, parents were burning their children alive as offerings. The law had forbidden it plainly: You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech (Lev 18:21).

And then a phrase that is almost unbearable: which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind. God says the thought never entered his mind. Whatever these people told themselves about pleasing a god, it had no connection whatever to the God who was speaking. Religion untethered from revelation does not drift toward kindness.

Two things follow. First, every generation should ask what it does to its own children and calls necessary. Second, notice where this valley leads. The Valley of Hinnom — Ge-Hinnom — became the New Testament word for hell itself, the place Jesus described as one where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched (Mark 9:48). The name of a real ravine where children burned became the name for final judgment. The Bible's picture of hell was first a place human beings built.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it will no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter; for they will bury in Topheth, because there is no room elsewhere. And the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the air, and for the beasts of the earth, and none will frighten them away. And I will silence in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, for the land shall become a waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it will no more be called Topheth, or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter; for they will bury in Topheth, because there is no room elsewhere.

The punishment takes the shape of the crime, as it did in 5:19. The valley where they killed their children becomes the valley where their own dead are buried, so many that the graveyards overflow into it. The renaming is God's verdict written on the map.

And the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the air, and for the beasts of the earth, and none will frighten them away.

To be left unburied was the ultimate disgrace in that world. None will frighten them away — there will not even be anyone left to wave off the birds.

And I will silence in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, for the land shall become a waste."

The chapter ends not with an image of violence but with silence. No laughter in the streets, and no weddings. Of all the sounds God could name as the mark of a living community, he chooses the voices of a bride and bridegroom: the sound of people betting on a future.

That is what judgment takes away, and it is how John describes the fall of Babylon at the end of the Bible: the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more (Rev 18:23).

But this is the God who later says to these same exiles that he will bring back into this ruined land the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride (33:11), because his purpose was never the silence. Jeremiah preached in the temple gate that the house would fall. It did. And the one who quoted this sermon in the same courts went out and was himself destroyed, so that the wedding could be held after all.

7.title: The Temple Sermon: Do Not Trust in Deceptive Words
7.overview:
Jeremiah is sent to the temple gate to preach to worshippers on their way in: amend your ways and I will let you stay, and do not trust the chant the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD (vv. 1-4). The conditions are true justice, protection of the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow, no innocent blood and no other gods (vv. 5-7).

They break the commandments and then stand in God's house claiming deliverance, treating the temple as a robbers' hideout (vv. 8-11). So they are sent to look at the ruins of Shiloh, where God's name first dwelt: the temple will go the same way (vv. 12-15). Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for them, while whole families work together baking cakes for the queen of heaven, harming themselves more than they provoke God (vv. 16-20).

Sacrifices were never the first command; obedience was (vv. 21-24). God sent prophets persistently for centuries and each generation did worse (vv. 25-26). Jeremiah is told he will not be listened to, and that truth has perished (vv. 27-29). They have defiled the temple and burned their children at Topheth, which God never commanded and which never came into his mind (vv. 30-31); so it will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, and the voices of bridegroom and bride will be silenced (vv. 32-34).
7.theology:
Religious privilege guarantees nothing: true words about God's house became deceptive words when used as a shield for unrepentance (vv. 4, 8; Matt 7:26-27). God ties his presence to repentance and to justice for the weakest (vv. 5-7), and refuses to let worship and ethics be separated (vv. 9-11).

Shiloh proves that God will destroy a place he chose when it becomes a charm (vv. 12-15). Sacrifice was given inside the covenant to serve obedience, never to replace it (vv. 21-23; 1 Sam 15:22; Hos 6:6; Isa 1:13-17; Amos 5:24). Sin's damage falls first on the sinner (v. 19), and God's wrath is love's response to people destroying themselves and their children.

Prayer for a people can be forbidden when refusal has hardened (v. 16; 1 John 5:16), and faithfulness, not results, is the standard for the messenger (v. 27). Jesus took this sermon up in the same courts (Matt 21:13) and went to his death there, so that the silenced wedding might be restored (33:11).
7.examples:
Preaching at the door to people already on their way into church.

A chant of true words used as a shield.

A den: not where the robbery happens, but where robbers feel safe afterwards.

A twenty-mile walk to look at the ruins of Shiloh.

A family with a job each, working together on idolatry.

A city with no wedding music left in it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bones of kings, officials, priests, prophets and people will be taken from their tombs (v. 1) and spread before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, unburied, as dung on the surface of the ground (v. 2). And of the survivors, Death shall be preferred to life (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The gods they served become the witnesses of their shame, and the living envy the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: "At that time, declares the LORD, the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of its officials, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be brought out of their tombs. And they shall be spread before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after, and which they have sought and worshiped. And they shall not be gathered or buried. They shall be as dung on the surface of the ground. Death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family in all the places where I have driven them, declares the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"At that time, declares the LORD, the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of its officials, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem shall be brought out of their tombs.

Five times the bones, tolling through the sentence: kings, officials, priests, prophets, people. The same five groups the book keeps naming, now listed as skeletons. Death has levelled the hierarchy, and the invaders will loot the graves.

And they shall be spread before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after, and which they have sought and worshiped. And they shall not be gathered or buried. They shall be as dung on the surface of the ground.

Four verbs for their devotion — loved, served, gone after, sought and worshiped — and then the bones are laid out under those same stars. The gods they gave their lives to will watch them rot, and do nothing, because they were only ever lights in the sky.

That is the logic of this passage: idols do not merely fail to save; they become the audience of the disaster. Whatever a person has given himself to will be standing there at the end, mute.

Death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family in all the places where I have driven them, declares the LORD of hosts.

And for the survivors, life becomes worse than death. Scripture does not moralise about that or soften it. It is the plainest statement of what exile will feel like from inside.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When men fall, do they not rise again? If one turns away, does he not return? (v. 4). Yet this people holds fast to deceit, and no one asks What have I done?, each rushing on like a horse plunging headlong into battle (vv. 5-6). The migrating birds keep their seasons, but my people know not the rules of the LORD (v. 7). They claim wisdom while the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie (vv. 8-9). From least to greatest everyone is greedy; the wound is healed lightly with Peace, peace; and they cannot blush (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The instinct to get up after a fall has died, the calendar of the birds shames them, and even the Scriptures have been handled into a lie.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall say to them, Thus says the LORD: When men fall, do they not rise again? If one turns away, does he not return? Why then has this people turned away in perpetual backsliding? They hold fast to deceit; they refuse to return. I have paid attention and listened, but they have not spoken rightly; no man relents of his evil, saying, 'What have I done?' Everyone turns to his own course, like a horse plunging headlong into battle. Even the stork in the heavens knows her times, and the turtledove, swallow, and crane keep the time of their coming, but my people know not the rules of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You shall say to them, Thus says the LORD: When men fall, do they not rise again? If one turns away, does he not return?

Two questions drawn from ordinary life, and both expect the answer yes. A man who trips gets up. A traveller who takes a wrong turning goes back. Nobody lies in the road on principle, and nobody keeps walking the wrong way once he knows.

Why then has this people turned away in perpetual backsliding? They hold fast to deceit; they refuse to return.

The word perpetual is the sting. Not a fall but a way of life; not a wrong turning but a direction. And the grip is the wrong way round: they hold fast to deceit, clinging to the thing that is destroying them.

I have paid attention and listened, but they have not spoken rightly; no man relents of his evil, saying, 'What have I done?' Everyone turns to his own course, like a horse plunging headlong into battle.

God says he has been listening — leaning in, waiting to catch one sentence. And the sentence he is listening for is short: What have I done? Four words, and nobody says them.

Sit with that for a moment. God is not waiting for an explanation, a defence or a plan for improvement. He is waiting for the question people ask when they finally see their own behaviour from outside. It is the question the prodigal asked in a pig field, and the tax collector's prayer is its twin.

Instead: like a horse plunging headlong into battle. A warhorse in a charge cannot be reasoned with, cannot stop and will not turn. It is the perfect picture of momentum — a life with speed, direction and no brakes.

Even the stork in the heavens knows her times, and the turtledove, swallow, and crane keep the time of their coming, but my people know not the rules of the LORD.

Now look up. The migrating birds leave and return on time, every year, without instruction. The ESV notes that the name rendered crane is uncertain, and that rules may be rendered "just decrees". The point does not depend on the details: creatures with no reasoning keep God's calendar, and people made in his image do not know his ways. Isaiah said it with farm animals: The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know (Isa 1:3).

verseByVerse.quote: "How can you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us'? But behold, the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie. The wise men shall be put to shame; they shall be dismayed and taken; behold, they have rejected the word of the LORD, so what wisdom is in them? Therefore I will give their wives to others and their fields to conquerors, because from the least to the greatest everyone is greedy for unjust gain; from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace. Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among the fallen; when I punish them, they shall be overthrown, says the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"How can you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us'? But behold, the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie.

Here is a claim that was perfectly true and completely hollow: the law of the LORD is with us. They had the scrolls. Josiah's reform had rediscovered the book. Possession of Scripture had become a credential.

And then the charge, which is aimed at the professionals: the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie. The scribes copied and taught the text. God does not accuse them of losing it but of turning it into something false — presumably by the way they explained it, applied it and used it to underwrite what the nation wanted to do.

Scripture can be handled into a lie without a word of it being altered. Verses arranged to bless what God condemns, comfort detached from repentance, technical study that never asks for obedience: the pen is lying while every letter it copies is accurate. Anyone who teaches the Bible should read verse 8 once a year.

The wise men shall be put to shame; they shall be dismayed and taken; behold, they have rejected the word of the LORD, so what wisdom is in them?

The question answers itself. Wisdom that has rejected God's word has removed its own foundation, however impressive the structure looks.

Therefore I will give their wives to others and their fields to conquerors, because from the least to the greatest everyone is greedy for unjust gain; from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace. Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush. Therefore they shall fall among the fallen; when I punish them, they shall be overthrown, says the LORD.

These three verses repeat 6:13-15 almost word for word, and the repetition is the message. The sermon has already been preached; nothing has changed; so it is preached again, unaltered. Ezekiel used another image for the same men, prophets who say 'Peace,' when there is no peace and then whitewash the wall the people have built (Ezek 13:10).

A preacher who has to say the same thing twice to the same people is not necessarily failing. Jeremiah did it, and it was God's idea.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — No Grapes on the Vine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God comes to gather there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree (v. 13). The people answer by shutting themselves in the fortified cities with poisoned water (v. 14): We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror (v. 15). Horses snort at Dan, the land quakes (v. 16), and God sends serpents, adders that cannot be charmed (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The harvest God looked for is not there, and the remedies people reach for are poison and panic.

verseByVerse.quote: When I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered, and what I gave them has passed away from them." Why do we sit still? Gather together; let us go into the fortified cities and perish there, for the LORD our God has doomed us to perish and has given us poisoned water to drink, because we have sinned against the LORD. We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror. "The snorting of their horses is heard from Dan; at the sound of the neighing of their stallions the whole land quakes. They come and devour the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it. For behold, I am sending among you serpents, adders that cannot be charmed, and they shall bite you," declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered, and what I gave them has passed away from them."

God comes to his vineyard at harvest and finds nothing: no grapes, no figs, not even green leaves. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew here is uncertain, but the picture is unmistakable, and it is the picture Jesus acted out when he came to a leafy fig tree in Jerusalem and found no fruit on it.

Notice the last clause: what I gave them has passed away from them. The gifts have gone. That is often how judgment begins — not with a blow but with an absence.

Why do we sit still? Gather together; let us go into the fortified cities and perish there, for the LORD our God has doomed us to perish and has given us poisoned water to drink, because we have sinned against the LORD.

The people speak, and it is almost repentance. They name the cause correctly — because we have sinned against the LORD — and then act on despair rather than on that knowledge, shutting themselves into walled towns to die. An accurate diagnosis without hope produces fatalism, which looks like humility and is not.

We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror.

This is what the Peace, peace preaching of verse 11 finally delivers. People were promised healing and handed terror. False comfort is not a harmless kindness; there are casualties, and they are the ones who believed it.

"The snorting of their horses is heard from Dan; at the sound of the neighing of their stallions the whole land quakes. They come and devour the land and all that fills it, the city and those who dwell in it.

Sound again before sight, as in chapter 6: cavalry heard from the northern border, and the ground shaking. Dan was the proverbial far north; the enemy is inside the country.

For behold, I am sending among you serpents, adders that cannot be charmed, and they shall bite you," declares the LORD.

Snake charmers were a familiar sight, and their whole trade was managing danger. These serpents cannot be charmed. There is a point at which the techniques that have always worked stop working, and nothing in the repertoire will talk the danger down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Is There No Balm in Gilead?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me (v. 18). The people cry, Is the LORD not in Zion? Is her King not in her?, and God answers with their idols (v. 19). Then the saddest line in the book: The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved (v. 20). The prophet is wounded with their wound (v. 21) and asks, Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The medicine exists and the doctor is available; what is missing is any willingness to be treated.

verseByVerse.quote: My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me. Behold, the cry of the daughter of my people from the length and breadth of the land: "Is the LORD not in Zion? Is her King not in her?" "Why have they provoked me to anger with their carved images and with their foreign idols?" "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn, and dismay has taken hold on me. Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?
verseByVerse.commentary:
My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me.

The prophet again, and the ESV notes that the Hebrew of this line is uncertain. What comes through is plain enough: joy gone, grief arrived, heart sick. He has been preaching this judgment for chapters, and it is making him ill.

Behold, the cry of the daughter of my people from the length and breadth of the land: "Is the LORD not in Zion? Is her King not in her?" "Why have they provoked me to anger with their carved images and with their foreign idols?"

Two voices in one verse. The people cry out the theology they have always relied on: Is the LORD not in Zion? He lives here. He is our King. This cannot be happening.

And God answers the question with a question: then why the carved images? Their confidence rested on his presence while their affections rested elsewhere. You cannot claim a God as your security and treat him as optional.

"The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved."

One of the most haunting sentences in Scripture, and it is the people's own. In an agricultural year there is a window: the grain ripens, the harvest is gathered, and after that nothing more will grow. The window has shut, the barns are not full, and winter is coming. We are not saved.

Opportunity has a season. That is not a threat invented by preachers; it is how time works, and everyone knows it in farming, in health, in relationships. Paul makes the same point with urgency rather than gloom: now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2). The sentence in Jeremiah is what it sounds like to say it too late.

For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn, and dismay has taken hold on me.

He does not stand outside their loss. The wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded. Their injury is his injury, and the verse makes no distinction between them.

Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?

Gilead, east of the Jordan, was known for a medicinal resin traded across the region. Ask the question the way the verse asks it. Is there no balm? Of course there is. Is there no physician? There is. Then why is this patient not healed?

The answer the whole book has been giving: because she will not be treated. The wound has been bandaged lightly by men who called it peace, and the physician who could actually heal it has been refused. Jesus said, Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners (Mark 2:17). The one thing that keeps a person from the doctor is the conviction that nothing much is wrong.

8.title: Is There No Balm in Gilead?
8.overview:
The tombs of Judah's kings, officials, priests, prophets and people will be opened and their bones spread before the sun, moon and stars they worshipped, unburied; the survivors will prefer death to life (vv. 1-3).

Men who fall get up and travellers who go wrong turn back, but this people backslides perpetually and no one says What have I done? (vv. 4-6). Migrating birds keep their seasons while God's people do not know his rules (v. 7). They claim to be wise and to have the law, but the scribes' pen has made it a lie (vv. 8-9). Then the words of 6:13-15 are repeated unchanged: greed from least to greatest, false dealing from prophet to priest, the wound healed lightly with Peace, peace, and no ability to blush (vv. 10-12).

God comes for fruit and finds none (v. 13). The people shut themselves into fortified cities to perish, having looked for peace and received terror (vv. 14-15). Cavalry is heard from Dan, and serpents come that cannot be charmed (vv. 16-17). The prophet's joy is gone (v. 18); the people ask whether the LORD is not in Zion, and God asks about their idols (v. 19); and they say, The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved (v. 20). Wounded with their wound, Jeremiah asks whether there is no balm in Gilead and no physician there (vv. 21-22).
8.theology:
Idols cannot save and end as witnesses of their worshippers' ruin (vv. 1-2). Repentance begins with a question almost no one asks: What have I done? (v. 6). Creation keeps God's order while his people do not (v. 7; Isa 1:3).

Scripture can be handled into a lie without a word being altered (v. 8), and comfort preached over an untreated wound produces casualties (vv. 11, 15; Ezek 13:10).

Opportunity has a season, and it can close (v. 20; 2 Cor 6:2). The remedy exists — there is balm and there is a physician (v. 22) — and the barrier is the refusal to be treated (Mark 2:17). The prophet does not stand outside the grief he announces (vv. 18, 21).
8.examples:
Stars that were worshipped, looking down on the bones of the worshippers.

Four words nobody says: what have I done?

A warhorse in a charge, with speed, direction and no brakes.

Storks keeping a calendar that people have lost.

Every letter copied accurately, and the pen still lying.

The harvest gone, the barns empty, and winter coming.
