verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Why Does the Way of the Wicked Prosper?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? (v. 1). God himself planted them, and they thrive, though he is near in their mouth and far from their heart (v. 2). Jeremiah asks to be tested and asks that they be pulled out like sheep for the slaughter (v. 3), while the land mourns and the beasts are swept away because men said, He will not see our latter end (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet brings his hardest question to God rather than about him, and concedes God's righteousness before arguing.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all who are treacherous thrive? You plant them, and they take root; they grow and produce fruit; you are near in their mouth and far from their heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all who are treacherous thrive?

This is the second of Jeremiah's confessions, and notice how it begins. Before he asks anything he settles the question of who is in the right: Righteous are you, O LORD. Whatever the answer turns out to be, God is not the defendant.

And then he argues anyway. Yet I would plead my case before you. The verb is legal: he wants to lay the matter out as an advocate would. Scripture is not embarrassed by this. The complaint is addressed to God, not circulated behind his back, and that is the difference between lament and cynicism.

The question itself is the oldest one believers ask. Job asked it — Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power? (Job 21:7). Habakkuk asked it more sharply — why do you idly look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he? (Hab 1:13). And Asaph nearly lost his faith over it until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end (Ps 73:17).

Jeremiah's version has a personal edge. He has just learned that his neighbours want him dead (11:21). The wicked in view are not distant villains; they are the men who threatened him, and they are doing well.

You plant them, and they take root; they grow and produce fruit; you are near in their mouth and far from their heart.

He does not soften it: You plant them. Their success is not in spite of God; it comes from his hand. That is harder than saying evil men flourish by luck, and it is the truth this book keeps insisting on.

Then the sentence that pins the whole problem: you are near in their mouth and far from their heart. They talk about God constantly. His name is in their conversation, their oaths, their worship — and nowhere near the centre of them. That is what enrages the prophet. Not open atheism, which at least is honest, but a religion that keeps God on the lips and out of the life, and prospers doing it.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, know me; you see me, and test my heart toward you. Pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and set them apart for the day of slaughter. How long will the land mourn and the grass of every field wither? For the evil of those who dwell in it the beasts and the birds are swept away, because they said, "He will not see our latter end."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, O LORD, know me; you see me, and test my heart toward you.

Having described men whose hearts are far from God, he offers his own for inspection. Test my heart toward you. This is the same appeal as 11:20, and it costs something: a man who asks God to examine him has given up the right to be selective about what is found.

It is also the only safe ground from which to complain about anyone else. Most of our indignation would not survive that sentence.

Pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and set them apart for the day of slaughter.

And then the prayer that makes modern readers wince. He asks God to prepare them for slaughter as a shepherd separates animals for the butcher.

Two things keep this from being mere vindictiveness. First, he asks God to do it rather than doing it himself; the prayer is a refusal to take revenge. Second, the men he is describing have plotted murder and will shortly preside over the ruin of a nation. To feel nothing about that is not holiness. The psalms are full of such prayers, and the New Testament records the souls under the altar asking, how long before you judge (Rev 6:10).

Still, Christians read it through a later word. Jeremiah's greater Son prayed for those who drove the nails, and the vengeance this prayer asks for fell on him instead, for all who will have it.

How long will the land mourn and the grass of every field wither? For the evil of those who dwell in it the beasts and the birds are swept away, because they said, "He will not see our latter end."

The damage is ecological before it is political: dead grass, animals and birds gone. Human sin bends the creation it lives in, as chapter 4 showed.

And the root of it is one sentence they say to themselves: He will not see our latter end. Not that God does not exist, but that he will not be watching when the account comes due. It is the creed of 5:12 in different words, and it is the belief that makes any wickedness possible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–6 — How Will You Compete with Horses?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's reply is not an answer but a harder question: If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses? And if in a safe land you are so trusting, what will you do in the thicket of the Jordan? (v. 5). And then the reason he needs the warning: even your brothers and the house of your father, even they have dealt treacherously with you, however friendly their words (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not soothe his servant; he tells him the race gets harder, and warns him about his own family.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses? And if in a safe land you are so trusting, what will you do in the thicket of the Jordan? For even your brothers and the house of your father, even they have dealt treacherously with you; they are in full cry after you; do not believe them, though they speak friendly words to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses? And if in a safe land you are so trusting, what will you do in the thicket of the Jordan?

God answers, and he does not answer the question. There is no explanation of why the wicked prosper — that will wait for a cross and an empty tomb. Instead he asks two questions of his own, and they are bracing rather than comforting.

You are out of breath from a footrace, and cavalry is coming. You are unsteady on open ground, and the country ahead is the thicket of the Jordan — the dense scrub along the river where lions lived, where a man could not see ten feet.

What is God doing? He is telling his servant that this is the easy part. Anathoth was the village; Jerusalem is coming. And implicit in the questions is a promise: he is not being asked to find the strength himself. The one asking is the one who said I am with you to deliver you (1:8) and who makes prophets into iron pillars (1:18).

There is pastoral wisdom here for anyone worn out by a small trouble. God's cure is not usually to remove it but to grow the person who is carrying it. Let us run with endurance the race that is set before us (Heb 12:1).

For even your brothers and the house of your father, even they have dealt treacherously with you; they are in full cry after you; do not believe them, though they speak friendly words to you."

And here is why he will need horses. It is not only the men of Anathoth; it is your brothers and the house of your father. His own family. In full cry after you is the language of a hunt, hounds giving tongue behind the fox.

The final instruction is the cruellest kindness in the chapter: do not believe them, though they speak friendly words to you. He must go on living among these people and not trust a word they say. David knew it: it is not an enemy who taunts me— then I could bear it, but my companion, my familiar friend (Ps 55:12-13). And of the Lord himself it is written that not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — I Have Forsaken My House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my heritage; I have given the beloved of my soul into the hands of her enemies (v. 7). His heritage has roared at him like a lion (v. 8); the birds of prey circle and the beasts are summoned (v. 9). Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard, making his pleasant portion a wilderness, but no man lays it to heart (vv. 10-11). The sword of the LORD devours from end to end (v. 12), and those who have sown wheat and have reaped thorns are ashamed of their harvest (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is God's own bereavement: he calls the people he is handing over the beloved of his soul.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my heritage; I have given the beloved of my soul into the hands of her enemies. My heritage has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has lifted up her voice against me; therefore I hate her. Is my heritage to me like a hyena's lair? Are the birds of prey against her all around? Go, assemble all the wild beasts; bring them to devour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my heritage; I have given the beloved of my soul into the hands of her enemies.

The voice changes, and it takes a moment to realise who is speaking. This is God, describing what he is doing, and every line is a wound.

My house — the temple. My heritage — the people and the land, his own portion, what he chose for himself out of all the earth. And then, unbearably, the beloved of my soul, handed over to enemies.

Whatever else is true of the judgment in this book, read verse 7 before saying that God is detached from it. He is giving away what he loves. The phrase is the language of a man surrendering his wife to men who will hurt her, and it is God's own description of the exile.

And it is the shape of something later. There came a day when God gave the beloved of his soul into the hands of his enemies, and that time the giving was not judgment on the one given but redemption for the ones who took him.

My heritage has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has lifted up her voice against me; therefore I hate her.

Now the line that stops the reader. The relationship has reversed: his own inheritance now roars at him like a predator. The word hate in covenant language is not a mood but a verdict — the formal rejection of a party who has broken the treaty. It sits in the same book as I have loved you with an everlasting love (31:3), and both are spoken to the same people.

Is my heritage to me like a hyena's lair? Are the birds of prey against her all around? Go, assemble all the wild beasts; bring them to devour.

Vultures circling and scavengers called in to the carcass. The summons is God's own: Go, assemble all the wild beasts. The armies of Babylon are the beasts, and they come at his whistle.

verseByVerse.quote: Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard; they have trampled down my portion; they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness. They have made it a desolation; desolate, it mourns to me. The whole land is made desolate, but no man lays it to heart. Upon all the bare heights in the desert destroyers have come, for the sword of the LORD devours from one end of the land to the other; no flesh has peace. They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns; they have tired themselves out but profit nothing. They shall be ashamed of their harvests because of the fierce anger of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard; they have trampled down my portion; they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness.

Shepherds again, and the accusation is that they wrecked what they were given to tend. They did not merely fail to protect the vineyard; they trampled it. Chapter 23 will bring these men into court by name.

Twice in one verse God calls it my portion, the share he took for himself. It is his loss they have caused.

They have made it a desolation; desolate, it mourns to me. The whole land is made desolate, but no man lays it to heart.

The land mourns to God, and no person does. That is the indictment in a line: the fields have more sense of what has happened than the people who farm them. No man lays it to heart — nobody is thinking about it, nobody is grieved, life goes on.

It is possible for a community to live through something catastrophic and simply not register it. Whole societies manage this, and so do individuals with their own souls.

Upon all the bare heights in the desert destroyers have come, for the sword of the LORD devours from one end of the land to the other; no flesh has peace.

The sword of the LORD: Babylon's blade, and God calls it his own. The invaders are instruments, which is why chapter 25 can turn and judge the instrument.

They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns; they have tired themselves out but profit nothing. They shall be ashamed of their harvests because of the fierce anger of the LORD."

A farmer's nightmare and a fitting last word for the section. Good seed in, thorns out; exhausting labour and nothing to show. The ESV notes that their harvests is in Hebrew "your", turning the line to face the reader directly.

It is the harvest of chapter 2 in the end: cisterns dug at enormous cost that hold no water, wheat sown that comes up thorns. Sin never produces what it advertises, and the bill for the labour still arrives.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Of the neighbouring nations who seized Israel's land God says, I will pluck them up from their land, and Judah with them (v. 14). And after I have plucked them up, I will again have compassion on them, bringing each back to his heritage (v. 15). If those nations learn to swear by the LORD's name as they once taught Israel to swear by Baal, then they shall be built up in the midst of my people (v. 16); if not, they will be uprooted (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The same hand that uproots replants, and the offer of a place among God's people is extended to the very nations that corrupted them.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD concerning all my evil neighbors who touch the heritage that I have given my people Israel to inherit: "Behold, I will pluck them up from their land, and I will pluck up the house of Judah from among them. And after I have plucked them up, I will again have compassion on them, and I will bring them again each to his heritage and each to his land. And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, 'As the LORD lives,' even as they taught my people to swear by Baal, then they shall be built up in the midst of my people. But if any nation will not listen, then I will utterly pluck it up and destroy it, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD concerning all my evil neighbors who touch the heritage that I have given my people Israel to inherit: "Behold, I will pluck them up from their land, and I will pluck up the house of Judah from among them.

The nations who moved in on Israel's land — Edom, Moab, Ammon and the rest — are now addressed. God calls them my evil neighbors, and the charge is that they touch the heritage that belongs to him. Whatever Judah deserved, the neighbours who profited by her fall are not innocent.

Notice that the same verb falls on both: I will pluck them up, and I will pluck up the house of Judah from among them. God's people are not exempted from the uprooting. Being his does not mean being spared.

And after I have plucked them up, I will again have compassion on them, and I will bring them again each to his heritage and each to his land.

And here the chapter turns. After I have plucked them up, I will again have compassion. The uprooting is not the end of the sentence. Chapter 1 gave six verbs, four of them destructive and two constructive, and this is the pattern working out: the same hand that pulls up will plant again.

Read carefully who receives the compassion. In verse 14 the ones plucked up are the nations; here each to his heritage and each to his land reaches beyond Judah to them as well.

And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, 'As the LORD lives,' even as they taught my people to swear by Baal, then they shall be built up in the midst of my people.

This is an astonishing sentence, and it is easy to read past. The nations that taught Israel to swear by Baal — the very source of the corruption this book has spent twelve chapters describing — are offered a place. Not on the edge, but built up in the midst of my people.

The condition is real: diligently learn the ways of my people, and swear by the LORD's name. Learning runs in the opposite direction from before, and the people who once exported idolatry now have to be taught the fear of God by the nation they corrupted.

That is the gospel's shape, centuries early. Paul describes Gentiles as a wild olive shoot grafted in among the others who share the root's nourishment, with a warning not to be arrogant toward the natural branches (Rom 11:17-18). James summed up the council in Jerusalem the same way: God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name (Acts 15:14).

But if any nation will not listen, then I will utterly pluck it up and destroy it, declares the LORD."

The offer is genuine and it is not automatic. The condition that governs Judah governs the nations too: listening. The chapter that began with a question about God's fairness ends by showing him opening his household to his enemies, on the same terms he has been offering his own people since chapter 3.

12.title: Why Does the Way of the Wicked Prosper?
12.overview:
Jeremiah brings God his hardest question, first conceding that God is righteous: why does the way of the wicked prosper, when God himself planted them and they keep him near in their mouths and far from their hearts (vv. 1-2)? He offers his own heart for testing, asks that the wicked be set apart for slaughter, and describes a land mourning because men have decided God will not see their end (vv. 3-4).

God does not answer the question. He asks two of his own: if a footrace has worn you out, how will you race horses, and if you stumble in safe country, what will you do in the Jordan thicket (v. 5)? Even Jeremiah's brothers and his father's house have turned on him, however friendly their words (v. 6).

Then God laments what he is doing: he has forsaken his house and given the beloved of my soul into enemy hands (vv. 7-9). Shepherds have trampled his vineyard, the land mourns and no one takes it to heart, and those who sowed wheat have reaped thorns (vv. 10-13). Finally the nations who seized Israel's heritage will themselves be uprooted — and then shown compassion: if they will learn to swear by the LORD's name as they once taught Israel to swear by Baal, they will be built up among his people (vv. 14-17).
12.theology:
Complaint brought to God, with his righteousness conceded first, is an act of faith rather than rebellion (v. 1; Job 21:7; Hab 1:13; Ps 73:17). Nominal religion keeps God in the mouth and far from the heart (v. 2), and the creed that makes any wickedness possible is that God will not see the end of it (v. 4).

God's answer to a weary servant is not relief but enlargement: the race gets harder and he must grow (v. 5; Heb 12:1). Asking God for vengeance is a way of refusing to take it (v. 3).

Judgment costs God: he hands over the beloved of my soul (v. 7) — language later fulfilled when he gave his Son into the hands of enemies for our salvation. The uprooting is followed by compassion (v. 15), and the nations that corrupted Israel are offered a place among God's people on the same condition of listening (vv. 16-17; Rom 11:17-18; Acts 15:14).
12.examples:
Conceding that God is in the right before arguing with him.

A faith kept on the lips and nowhere near the centre.

Out of breath from a footrace, with cavalry coming.

Hounds in full cry, and they are your own family.

Fields that mourn while the people who farm them notice nothing.

The nations that taught Israel to swear by Baal, offered a place in the household.

I will not pity or spare or have compassion, that I should not destroy them.'"<sup>15</sup>Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the LORD has spoken.<sup>16</sup>Give glory to the LORD your God before he brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the twilight mountains, and while you look for light he turns it into gloom and makes it deep darkness.<sup>17</sup>But if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride; my eyes will weep bitterly and run down with tears, because the LORD's flock has been taken captive.<sup>18</sup>Say to the king and the queen mother: "Take a lowly seat, for your beautiful crown has come down from your head."<sup>19</sup>The cities of the Negeb are shut up, with none to open them; all Judah is taken into exile, wholly taken into exile.<sup>20</sup>"Lift up your eyes and see those who come from the north. Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will it be before you are made clean?"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Jeremiah to buy a linen loincloth, wear it, and not wash it (vv. 1-2), then to hide it in a cleft of the rock by the Euphrates (vv. 3-5). After many days he digs it up and finds it spoiled; it was good for nothing (vv. 6-7). The meaning follows: Even so will I spoil the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem (vv. 8-10), For as the loincloth clings to the waist of a man, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, to be a people, a name, a praise, and a glory, but they would not listen (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: God made his people to cling to him as closely as clothing; pride left to rot by a foreign river is what became of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD to me, "Go and buy a linen loincloth and put it around your waist, and do not dip it in water." So I bought a loincloth according to the word of the LORD, and put it around my waist. And the word of the LORD came to me a second time, "Take the loincloth that you have bought, which is around your waist, and arise, go to the Euphrates and hide it there in a cleft of the rock." So I went and hid it by the Euphrates, as the LORD commanded me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD to me, "Go and buy a linen loincloth and put it around your waist, and do not dip it in water." So I bought a loincloth according to the word of the LORD, and put it around my waist.

Jeremiah's preaching now becomes theatre. He is told to buy a piece of clothing, wear it, and never wash it. Linen was the fabric of priestly garments, and this is the most intimate article of dress there is, worn against the skin under everything else.

Prophets were regularly asked to act out their message. It makes the word visible, and it costs the messenger his dignity: a man walking round Jerusalem in a garment he is forbidden to wash becomes the sermon.

And the word of the LORD came to me a second time, "Take the loincloth that you have bought, which is around your waist, and arise, go to the Euphrates and hide it there in a cleft of the rock." So I went and hid it by the Euphrates, as the LORD commanded me.

The second instruction is stranger than the first, and expensive. The Euphrates is the river of Babylon, hundreds of miles away — the direction from which the armies come, and the place to which the people will be carried. He obeys without recorded comment: So I went and hid it.

Obedience in this book is rarely explained in advance. God tells him what to do and only later tells him what it means, which is how most obedience works.

verseByVerse.quote: And after many days the LORD said to me, "Arise, go to the Euphrates, and take from there the loincloth that I commanded you to hide there." Then I went to the Euphrates, and dug, and I took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it. And behold, the loincloth was spoiled; it was good for nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after many days the LORD said to me, "Arise, go to the Euphrates, and take from there the loincloth that I commanded you to hide there." Then I went to the Euphrates, and dug, and I took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it. And behold, the loincloth was spoiled; it was good for nothing.

The journey is made a second time, and the prophet kneels in the mud by a foreign river digging up his own underwear. What he lifts out is rotten: stained, weakened, falling apart. Good for nothing.

That is the phrase to carry into the interpretation. Not damaged but still serviceable; useless. A garment that can no longer do the one thing a garment does.

And notice where the ruin happened: not in Jerusalem, but buried by the Euphrates. What destroys this people will be their long, deliberate burial of themselves among the nations whose gods they wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "Thus says the LORD: Even so will I spoil the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem. This evil people, who refuse to hear my words, who stubbornly follow their own heart and have gone after other gods to serve them and worship them, shall be like this loincloth, which is good for nothing. For as the loincloth clings to the waist of a man, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, declares the LORD, that they might be for me a people, a name, a praise, and a glory, but they would not listen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the word of the LORD came to me: "Thus says the LORD: Even so will I spoil the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem.

Now the meaning, and the target is named: pride, twice. Not first their idolatry or their injustice, but the self-satisfaction underneath both. The linen was proud stuff, priestly and fine. God says he will rot it.

This evil people, who refuse to hear my words, who stubbornly follow their own heart and have gone after other gods to serve them and worship them, shall be like this loincloth, which is good for nothing.

Three habits are listed, and they run in order: refusing to hear, following their own heart, going after other gods. That is the sequence every time. Stop listening, and you will be led by your own heart; follow your heart long enough, and it will find you a god.

For as the loincloth clings to the waist of a man, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, declares the LORD, that they might be for me a people, a name, a praise, and a glory, but they would not listen.

Here is the tenderness at the centre of a harsh chapter. The point of the sign is clinging. That is what God made them for: to be as close to him as clothing is to skin, in contact all day, unnoticed by others but never apart. Moses gave the same command in plain words — You shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him (Deut 10:20).

And four words say what he wanted out of it: a people, a name, a praise, and a glory. Not servants who keep the rules, but a people who are his ornament, the thing he is pleased to be seen wearing. It is the same astonishing idea Paul applies to the church, presented to Christ in splendour.

Then the ending: but they would not listen. Clothing that will not stay close to the body is buried in mud by a foreign river and rots.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — Every Jar Filled with Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A saying everyone knows — Every jar shall be filled with wine — is met with the obvious reply (v. 12). Then God turns it: Behold, I will fill with drunkenness all the inhabitants of this land, kings, priests, prophets and people (v. 13), And I will dash them one against another, fathers and sons together, without pity (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: A proverb about full jars becomes a picture of a nation staggering and smashed against itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall speak to them this word: 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, "Every jar shall be filled with wine."' And they will say to you, 'Do we not indeed know that every jar will be filled with wine?' Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I will fill with drunkenness all the inhabitants of this land: the kings who sit on David's throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And I will dash them one against another, fathers and sons together, declares the LORD. I will not pity or spare or have compassion, that I should not destroy them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You shall speak to them this word: 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, "Every jar shall be filled with wine."' And they will say to you, 'Do we not indeed know that every jar will be filled with wine?'

God gives him a proverb so obvious that the reply is predictable: of course jars get filled with wine; that is what jars are for. You can hear the impatience in it — the crowd is tired of this man and his sayings.

Then you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, I will fill with drunkenness all the inhabitants of this land: the kings who sit on David's throne, the priests, the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

And the platitude turns in their hands. Yes, every jar will be filled — and you are the jars, and what fills you is not wine but drunkenness: confusion, staggering, the loss of judgment that comes over a whole society when God gives it up to its own choices.

The list runs from David's throne down to the ordinary citizen. Nobody is sober.

And I will dash them one against another, fathers and sons together, declares the LORD. I will not pity or spare or have compassion, that I should not destroy them.'"

Full jars smashed together: the sound is of pottery breaking. It is a picture of a nation turning on itself under pressure — fathers and sons together — which is exactly what the last years of Judah looked like, with factions destroying one another while an empire waited outside.

The three verbs of withheld mercy are among the heaviest in the book. They are not God's final word to this people; chapter 31 is. They are his word to a generation that has used his patience as permission.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Give Glory Before the Darkness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the LORD has spoken (v. 15). Give glory to the LORD your God before he brings darkness, while there is still light to walk in (v. 16). If they will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride (v. 17). The king and the queen mother are told to take a lowly seat, for your beautiful crown has come down from your head (v. 18), and the cities of the Negeb are shut up while Judah goes into exile (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: There is a window of light in which glory can still be given to God, and pride is what keeps a people from using it.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the LORD has spoken. Give glory to the LORD your God before he brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the twilight mountains, and while you look for light he turns it into gloom and makes it deep darkness. But if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride; my eyes will weep bitterly and run down with tears, because the LORD's flock has been taken captive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear and give ear; be not proud, for the LORD has spoken. Give glory to the LORD your God before he brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the twilight mountains, and while you look for light he turns it into gloom and makes it deep darkness.

After the smashing, an appeal — and this is the pattern of the whole book. The door is still open while the sentence is being announced.

The picture is of a traveller caught out in the hills. Anyone who has been on a mountain at dusk knows how fast usable light disappears and how quickly the ground becomes treacherous. Give glory to the LORD your God before that happens. Give it now, while you can still see the path.

Jesus used the same image about himself, in the last days before the cross: The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you (John 12:35). Light is a season, not a permanent condition, and the sensible thing is to move while it lasts.

And notice what standing in the way is: be not proud. Pride is what keeps a person from giving glory, because giving glory means admitting whose it is.

But if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride; my eyes will weep bitterly and run down with tears, because the LORD's flock has been taken captive.

Here is the prophet again, and the tears are not for effect: in secret, where nobody would see them. A man can be angry in public and broken in private, and that combination is the mark of someone who actually loves the people he is warning.

He weeps for your pride — grieving not only the coming disaster but the thing that causes it. And he calls them the LORD's flock, still, in the sentence that describes their captivity.

verseByVerse.quote: Say to the king and the queen mother: "Take a lowly seat, for your beautiful crown has come down from your head." The cities of the Negeb are shut up, with none to open them; all Judah is taken into exile, wholly taken into exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Say to the king and the queen mother: "Take a lowly seat, for your beautiful crown has come down from your head."

A specific message for two named seats. The queen mother held real authority in Judah, and the pairing points to the young king Jehoiachin and his mother, who were carried to Babylon in 597 BC after a reign of three months.

Take a lowly seat is court language reversed: come down from the dais and sit on the floor. The crown has already fallen in God's telling, while it is still on the head.

The cities of the Negeb are shut up, with none to open them; all Judah is taken into exile, wholly taken into exile.

The Negeb is the far south, the part of the country furthest from the invasion route, and even there the towns are sealed with nobody to open them. The repetition — taken into exile, wholly taken into exile — is the sound of a door closing twice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–27 — Can the Ethiopian Change His Skin?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where is the flock that was given you, your beautiful flock? (vv. 20-21). When they ask Why have these things come upon me?, the answer is the greatness of their iniquity (v. 22). Then the question that exposes the whole problem: Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil (v. 23). They will be scattered like chaff, having forgotten me and trusted in lies (vv. 24-25), their shame exposed (vv. 26-27): How long will it be before you are made clean?
verseByVerse.theology: Habit has hardened into nature, so the command to do good cannot be obeyed — and the chapter ends with the question only God can answer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Lift up your eyes and see those who come from the north. Where is the flock that was given you, your beautiful flock? What will you say when they set as head over you those whom you yourself have taught to be friends to you? Will not pangs take hold of you like those of a woman in labor? And if you say in your heart, 'Why have these things come upon me?' it is for the greatness of your iniquity that your skirts are lifted up and you suffer violence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Lift up your eyes and see those who come from the north. Where is the flock that was given you, your beautiful flock?

The question is put to the leaders, and it is the question every shepherd dreads: where are the sheep? They were given you — entrusted, not owned — and they were beautiful. Now look north and count them.

Anyone with responsibility for others — a pastor, a parent, a teacher, an employer — will one day be asked some version of this.

What will you say when they set as head over you those whom you yourself have taught to be friends to you? Will not pangs take hold of you like those of a woman in labor?

The allies Judah cultivated will become her masters. The diplomacy of chapter 2 — drinking from the Nile and the Euphrates — ends with the foreign friends installed as rulers. Every accommodation made to gain their favour becomes a chain.

And if you say in your heart, 'Why have these things come upon me?' it is for the greatness of your iniquity that your skirts are lifted up and you suffer violence.

God answers the question before it is asked, as he did in 5:19 and 9:12. He refuses to let the catastrophe be mysterious. The imagery that follows is the public shaming of an adulteress, and it is deliberately hard to read: the prophets use it because covenant unfaithfulness is not a technical breach but a betrayal with a body.

verseByVerse.quote: Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil. I will scatter you like chaff driven by the wind from the desert.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil.

This is the most important sentence in the chapter and one of the sentences the whole book leans on, and it is a question with only one answer.

Two things are named that cannot alter themselves. A man's skin is what he was born with; a leopard's spots are not a decision. Neither is a fault — the verse is not about the Ethiopian or the leopard being wrong, but about them being fixed. And then the application lands: Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil. You can do good about as easily as a leopard can rearrange its coat.

Notice the word accustomed. This is not saying that people are born incapable of any decent act. It is saying that long practice has turned a habit into a nature. What was once chosen is now automatic, and the will that would have to choose differently is the very thing that has been shaped by the choosing.

The New Testament says it flatly: the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom 8:7-8). And Jesus, to a religious man at night: unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3). Not may not; cannot.

This is why moral appeals alone never save anyone, and why the whole book has been pleading with people who cannot do what is being asked. It sounds like despair, and it is the doorway to hope, because it drives the question to the only one who can answer it. What a leopard cannot do to itself, God can do to a person: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek 36:26), and in this book, a law written on the heart (31:33).

There is a quiet postscript in Acts. An Ethiopian sits in a chariot reading Isaiah, a man explains Jesus to him, and he goes on his way rejoicing (Acts 8:32-35). He did not change his skin. God changed his heart.

I will scatter you like chaff driven by the wind from the desert.

Chaff is what is left when the grain is gone: weightless, and the desert wind takes it. The ESV notes that you is in Hebrew "them". Either way the image is of a people with nothing solid left to hold them down.

verseByVerse.quote: This is your lot, the portion I have measured out to you, declares the LORD, because you have forgotten me and trusted in lies. I myself will lift up your skirts over your face, and your shame will be seen. I have seen your abominations, your adulteries and neighings, your lewd whorings, on the hills in the field. Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will it be before you are made clean?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is your lot, the portion I have measured out to you, declares the LORD, because you have forgotten me and trusted in lies.

Your lot, the portion I have measured out. In chapter 10 the LORD was the portion of Jacob (10:16) — he was their share. Now their share is exile. A people who would not have God as their portion receive another one, measured by him.

And the cause is two things: you have forgotten me and trusted in lies. Forgetting and trusting. Nobody believes nothing; whatever is forgotten is replaced.

I myself will lift up your skirts over your face, and your shame will be seen. I have seen your abominations, your adulteries and neighings, your lewd whorings, on the hills in the field.

The exposure imagery returns, and it is the punishment fitting the crime: what was done in secret on the hills will be made public. I have seen — the shame was visible to God long before it was visible to anyone else.

The word neighings recalls 5:8, where the men of the city were stallions after their neighbours' wives. The language is coarse because the behaviour was, and because the prophets refuse to let sin be described in terms that make it sound manageable.

Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will it be before you are made clean?"

The chapter ends on a question, and it is left hanging. How long will it be before you are made clean? After verse 23 the reader knows that the city cannot answer it: a people who cannot do good cannot wash themselves either.

So the question waits for God, and he answers it later in the same book: I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me (33:8). The one who asks how long is the one who will do the washing, and the cost of it appears at the far end of the story, when the Lamb of God takes away the sin of the world.

13.title: Can the Ethiopian Change His Skin?
13.overview:
God tells Jeremiah to buy a linen loincloth, wear it unwashed, and then bury it in a rock cleft by the Euphrates (vv. 1-5). Dug up after many days it is spoiled and good for nothing (vv. 6-7). So God will spoil the pride of Judah, a people who refuse to hear, follow their own hearts and serve other gods (vv. 8-10) — for he made Israel to cling to him as a loincloth clings to a man, to be for him a people, a name, a praise and a glory, and they would not listen (v. 11).

A proverb about jars being filled with wine becomes a sentence: God will fill the whole nation with drunkenness and dash them against one another without pity (vv. 12-14). Then an appeal: give glory to God before the darkness falls and the feet stumble on the mountains; if not, the prophet will weep in secret for their pride (vv. 15-17). The king and queen mother must take a lowly seat, and Judah goes wholly into exile (vv. 18-19).

The leaders are asked where their beautiful flock has gone, and told that the allies they courted will rule them (vv. 20-22). Then the question that explains everything: can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? No more can those accustomed to evil do good (v. 23). They will be scattered like chaff, their shame exposed, because they forgot God and trusted lies — and the chapter ends asking how long before they are made clean (vv. 24-27).
13.theology:
God made his people to cling to him as closely as clothing (v. 11; Deut 10:20), and their intended purpose was to be his people, name, praise and glory. Pride is what rots that closeness and what prevents glory being given (vv. 9, 15-17).

There is a window of light in which God may still be glorified, and it closes (v. 16; John 12:35-36). God refuses to let judgment appear mysterious; he states its cause (v. 22).

Verse 23 teaches the inability of the sinner: habit has become nature, so doing good is not merely difficult but impossible (Rom 8:7-8; John 3:3). That drives the need for what only God can give, a new heart and a law written within (Ezek 36:26; 31:33), and the closing question — how long before you are made clean — is answered by God himself (33:8).
13.examples:
A man made to preach by wearing an unwashed garment round the city.

Digging up your own clothing from the mud of a foreign river.

Clothing worn against the skin: in contact all day, unnoticed by others.

Full jars smashed against one another.

A traveller on a mountain as the usable light goes.

A leopard invited to rearrange its spots.

14.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought:<sup>2</sup>"Judah mourns, and her gates languish; her people lament on the ground, and the cry of Jerusalem goes up.<sup>3</sup>Her nobles send their servants for water; they come to the cisterns; they find no water; they return with their vessels empty; they are ashamed and confounded and cover their heads.<sup>4</sup>Because of the ground that is dismayed, since there is no rain on the land, the farmers are ashamed; they cover their heads.<sup>5</sup>Even the doe in the field forsakes her newborn fawn because there is no grass.<sup>6</sup>The wild donkeys stand on the bare heights; they pant for air like jackals; their eyes fail because there is no vegetation.<sup>7</sup>"Though our iniquities testify against us, act, O LORD, for your name's sake; for our backslidings are many; we have sinned against you.<sup>8</sup>O you hope of Israel, its savior in time of trouble, why should you be like a stranger in the land, like a traveler who turns aside to tarry for a night?<sup>9</sup>Why should you be like a man confused, like a mighty warrior who cannot save?
