verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought (v. 1). Judah mourns and Jerusalem cries out (v. 2); servants sent for water find no water; they return with their vessels empty and cover their heads (v. 3), and so do the farmers (v. 4). Even the animals suffer: the doe abandons her newborn fawn, and the wild donkeys pant for air like jackals because there is no vegetation (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The land itself preaches: empty vessels, ashamed farmers and animals abandoning their young.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought: "Judah mourns, and her gates languish; her people lament on the ground, and the cry of Jerusalem goes up. Her nobles send their servants for water; they come to the cisterns; they find no water; they return with their vessels empty; they are ashamed and confounded and cover their heads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought: "Judah mourns, and her gates languish; her people lament on the ground, and the cry of Jerusalem goes up.

A new section, and its subject is weather. The gates were where a town did its business and held its courts; when the gates languish, public life has stopped. People are sitting on the ground, which is the posture of mourning, and the noise of the city has become one long cry.

Drought was not a random misfortune in Israel's understanding. God had said at the start that the land's rain was tied to the covenant: the heavens over your head shall be bronze, and the earth under you shall be iron (Deut 28:23). A sky that gives nothing was a sermon everyone could feel.

Her nobles send their servants for water; they come to the cisterns; they find no water; they return with their vessels empty; they are ashamed and confounded and cover their heads.

Watch the sequence, because it is written like a short film: the order given, the walk to the cisterns, the search, the empty jars, the long walk back. And then the faces: ashamed and confounded, heads covered.

The detail that matters most is the cisterns. This is the book that defined the nation's sin as digging broken cisterns that can hold no water while abandoning the fountain of living waters (2:13). Now they go to their cisterns and find exactly what the metaphor promised. Sin's outcome eventually arrives in physical form, and the empty jar in a servant's hands is the picture of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Because of the ground that is dismayed, since there is no rain on the land, the farmers are ashamed; they cover their heads. Even the doe in the field forsakes her newborn fawn because there is no grass. The wild donkeys stand on the bare heights; they pant for air like jackals; their eyes fail because there is no vegetation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of the ground that is dismayed, since there is no rain on the land, the farmers are ashamed; they cover their heads.

Even the soil is said to be dismayed. The farmers cover their heads like the nobles' servants — the two ends of society making the same gesture, because the drought does not consult rank.

And notice the shame. A farmer whose field fails feels it as failure, though he did not make the weather. Anyone who has watched a harvest, a business or a body fail will recognise the instinct to cover the head.

Even the doe in the field forsakes her newborn fawn because there is no grass. The wild donkeys stand on the bare heights; they pant for air like jackals; their eyes fail because there is no vegetation.

Now the animals, and these two pictures are among the most affecting in the book. A doe abandons her newborn — an act against every instinct she has, and she does it because there is nothing to feed it with. Wild donkeys stand on the ridges with their heads up, panting, eyes failing.

Scripture keeps insisting that human sin damages more than humans. The creation that was subjected to futility groans (Rom 8:20-22), and here the groaning is a fawn left in the grass.

It is also, quietly, an argument. The animals have done nothing wrong and are suffering; the people have done a great deal wrong and are complaining. The drought is a mirror held up to a nation that has abandoned its own young in the valley of Hinnom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Act for Your Name's Sake
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Though our iniquities testify against us, act, O LORD, for your name's sake (v. 7). They call him O you hope of Israel, its savior in time of trouble and ask why he behaves like a stranger passing the night (vv. 8-9). God answers that They have loved to wander thus; they have not restrained their feet (v. 10), and tells Jeremiah, Do not pray for the welfare of this people (v. 11); fasting and offerings will not be accepted (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is theologically perfect and the feet have not changed direction, and God answers the feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "Though our iniquities testify against us, act, O LORD, for your name's sake; for our backslidings are many; we have sinned against you. O you hope of Israel, its savior in time of trouble, why should you be like a stranger in the land, like a traveler who turns aside to tarry for a night? Why should you be like a man confused, like a mighty warrior who cannot save? Yet you, O LORD, are in the midst of us, and we are called by your name; do not leave us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Though our iniquities testify against us, act, O LORD, for your name's sake; for our backslidings are many; we have sinned against you.

The people pray, and as prayer it is very good indeed. They do not argue that they deserve help. They concede the evidence — our iniquities testify against us — and then appeal to the one ground that is left: for your name's sake.

That is the highest form of prayer in the Old Testament. Moses used it at Sinai, Asaph used it after the temple was sacked — Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name's sake! (Ps 79:9) — and Daniel would use it in Babylon: we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy (Dan 9:18).

O you hope of Israel, its savior in time of trouble, why should you be like a stranger in the land, like a traveler who turns aside to tarry for a night?

The titles are exactly right: hope of Israel, savior in time of trouble. And the complaint is vivid. You are behaving like a tourist — someone who stops at an inn, sleeps, and is gone in the morning with no stake in the place. Why are you a visitor in your own country?

Why should you be like a man confused, like a mighty warrior who cannot save? Yet you, O LORD, are in the midst of us, and we are called by your name; do not leave us."

Bolder still: like a soldier who has lost his nerve. They are telling God that his reputation is suffering. And they end with the covenant itself — Yet you, O LORD, are in the midst of us, and we are called by your name — and a plea a child might make: do not leave us.

Read on its own, this prayer deserves an answer. Which is what makes the next verse so unsettling.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD concerning this people: "They have loved to wander thus; they have not restrained their feet; therefore the LORD does not accept them; now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins." The LORD said to me: "Do not pray for the welfare of this people. Though they fast, I will not hear their cry, and though they offer burnt offering and grain offering, I will not accept them. But I will consume them by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD concerning this people: "They have loved to wander thus; they have not restrained their feet; therefore the LORD does not accept them; now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins."

God does not answer the words. He answers the feet.

They have loved to wander — not drifted, loved it. They have not restrained their feet — the one thing repentance would have required, and it was never attempted. Beautiful prayers came out of the same city in which the shrines stayed open.

This is the lesson the chapter presses, and it is not that God is deaf. It is that words to God are measured against the direction of a life. The same book has already told us what God is listening for: one honest What have I done? (8:6), and a turning that follows it.

The LORD said to me: "Do not pray for the welfare of this people.

The third time (7:16; 11:14). Each time it is more specific, and each repetition tells us the prophet had gone on praying.

Though they fast, I will not hear their cry, and though they offer burnt offering and grain offering, I will not accept them. But I will consume them by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence."

Fasting, burnt offering, grain offering — the full range of religious response, refused. Isaiah heard the same from God: even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood (Isa 1:15).

These verses need care. They are not a general statement that God rejects sinners who come to him; the whole Bible says the opposite, and this book will end with a new covenant. They are about a people using worship as a lever while refusing to change course, and they exist to stop anyone treating prayer as a technique.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeremiah pleads that the prophets have promised assured peace in this place (v. 13). God replies, I did not send them, nor did I command them or speak to them (v. 14): by sword and famine those prophets will be consumed (v. 15), and the people who believed them will lie unburied in the streets (v. 16). Then the tears: Let my eyes run down with tears night and day for a people shattered with a great wound (v. 17), where both prophet and priest ply their trade through the land and have no knowledge (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: False comfort kills both the preacher and the congregation, and God orders the weeping over it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said: "Ah, Lord GOD, behold, the prophets say to them, 'You shall not see the sword, nor shall you have famine, but I will give you assured peace in this place.'" And the LORD said to me: "The prophets are prophesying lies in my name. I did not send them, nor did I command them or speak to them. They are prophesying to you a lying vision, worthless divination, and the deceit of their own minds. Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name although I did not send them, and who say, 'Sword and famine shall not come upon this land': By sword and famine those prophets shall be consumed. And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem, victims of famine and sword, with none to bury them—them, their wives, their sons, and their daughters. For I will pour out their evil upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I said: "Ah, Lord GOD, behold, the prophets say to them, 'You shall not see the sword, nor shall you have famine, but I will give you assured peace in this place.'"

Jeremiah tries one more argument, and it is a generous one: they were misled. Their preachers told them there would be no war and no hunger, and promised assured peace — the phrase has a confident, official ring to it.

It is the plea of a pastor who knows his people are not chiefly wicked but badly taught.

And the LORD said to me: "The prophets are prophesying lies in my name. I did not send them, nor did I command them or speak to them. They are prophesying to you a lying vision, worthless divination, and the deceit of their own minds.

God's answer is emphatic, and the denial is threefold: not sent, not commanded, not spoken to. Whatever those men were doing, God had no part in it.

And the last phrase names the source: the deceit of their own minds. They were not channelling demons; they were saying what they themselves found plausible and agreeable, and calling it the word of the LORD. That is how most false teaching is made — sincerity at work with no revelation behind it.

Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name although I did not send them, and who say, 'Sword and famine shall not come upon this land': By sword and famine those prophets shall be consumed.

The sentence fits the crime exactly: the men who said the sword would not come will fall to it. Teachers are judged by the standard they preached.

And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem, victims of famine and sword, with none to bury them—them, their wives, their sons, and their daughters. For I will pour out their evil upon them.

And here is the hard part of the answer to Jeremiah's plea. The congregation dies with the preachers. Being deceived is not treated as an acquittal, because they chose the men who told them what they wanted — my people love to have it so (5:31).

That puts a real responsibility on anyone who listens to teaching. Nobody will be able to say at the end that they were only doing what their church told them.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall say to them this word: 'Let my eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease, for the virgin daughter of my people is shattered with a great wound, with a very grievous blow. If I go out into the field, behold, those pierced by the sword! And if I enter the city, behold, the diseases of famine! For both prophet and priest ply their trade through the land and have no knowledge.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You shall say to them this word: 'Let my eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease, for the virgin daughter of my people is shattered with a great wound, with a very grievous blow.

God tells him what to say, and the message is a flood of tears. Notice that this is commanded: the weeping is part of the sermon, not a weakness in the preacher. A man who could announce this dry-eyed would be misrepresenting God, because God is not dry-eyed.

The virgin daughter of my people — the tenderest name he has for them, used at the moment of her greatest disgrace.

If I go out into the field, behold, those pierced by the sword! And if I enter the city, behold, the diseases of famine! For both prophet and priest ply their trade through the land and have no knowledge.'"

Two doors and no way out: outside the walls the war dead, inside them the starving. Any reader who has seen a siege, a famine or a bombed city knows this verse is not rhetoric.

And the final line puts the cause beside the effect: prophet and priest ply their trade — a phrase for business as usual — and have no knowledge. Religion carried on as a profession by men who do not know God, while the bodies pile up outside. The priest still takes the service; the prophet still gives the address.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Have you utterly rejected Judah? Does your soul loathe Zion? (v. 19). We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, and the iniquity of our fathers, for we have sinned against you (v. 20). They appeal to his name, his throne and his covenant (v. 21), and end where the chapter began: Are there any among the false gods of the nations that can bring rain?, We set our hope on you, for you do all these things (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Every word of the confession is right, which makes the answer in the next chapter the most sobering thing in the book.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you utterly rejected Judah? Does your soul loathe Zion? Why have you struck us down so that there is no healing for us? We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror. We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, and the iniquity of our fathers, for we have sinned against you. Do not spurn us, for your name's sake; do not dishonor your glorious throne; remember and do not break your covenant with us. Are there any among the false gods of the nations that can bring rain? Or can the heavens give showers? Are you not he, O LORD our God? We set our hope on you, for you do all these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you utterly rejected Judah? Does your soul loathe Zion? Why have you struck us down so that there is no healing for us? We looked for peace, but no good came; for a time of healing, but behold, terror.

The people pray again, and the questions are raw. Have you utterly rejected us? Does your soul loathe Zion? They quote back the promise of healing that was preached to them (8:15) and set it against what actually arrived.

We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, and the iniquity of our fathers, for we have sinned against you.

And here is the confession God asked for in chapter 3: Only acknowledge your guilt (3:13). It is all here — their own wickedness, their fathers' iniquity, the direct address we have sinned against you.

Do not spurn us, for your name's sake; do not dishonor your glorious throne; remember and do not break your covenant with us.

The appeal is to God's name, God's throne and God's covenant — three grounds, none of them their own merit. If a prayer could be marked as an exercise, this one scores full marks.

Are there any among the false gods of the nations that can bring rain? Or can the heavens give showers? Are you not he, O LORD our God? We set our hope on you, for you do all these things.

And it ends with sound theology about the weather. The Baals were rain gods; the whole point of serving them was showers. Now, in a drought, the people say what chapter 10 said: those things are nothing, and rain is yours. Zechariah puts it positively: Ask rain from the LORD in the season of the spring rain (Zech 10:1).

So the chapter ends with a faultless prayer. Every phrase is true; the doctrine is exact; the confession is explicit. And the first verse of chapter 15 refuses it.

That is the most sobering movement in the book, and it must be handled carefully. It does not teach that God turns away a broken heart — a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise. It teaches that words, even perfect words, are not repentance, and that a nation can learn to say the right things in a crisis while loving to wander (v. 10). The test is not the eloquence of the prayer but the direction of the feet afterwards.

And for anyone frightened by this passage, Lamentations — written by the same man over the ruins — is the answer: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning (Lam 3:22-23).

14.title: The Drought, and Prayers That Are Not Heard
14.overview:
A drought comes on Judah. Public life stops, servants sent for water return with empty vessels, farmers cover their heads, and even the doe abandons her fawn while wild donkeys pant on the bare heights (vv. 1-6).

The people pray well: they admit their iniquities and appeal to God's name, calling him the hope of Israel and asking why he acts like a stranger passing the night (vv. 7-9). God answers not the words but the feet — they have loved to wander — and forbids Jeremiah to pray for them; fasting and offerings will not be accepted (vv. 10-12).

Jeremiah pleads that the prophets promised peace; God replies that he never sent them, that they will fall by the sword they denied, and that the people who believed them will fall too (vv. 13-16). He is commanded to weep night and day over a shattered people whose prophets and priests ply their trade without knowledge (vv. 17-18). The chapter ends with a faultless prayer — confession of sin, appeal to God's name, throne and covenant, and the acknowledgement that only the LORD gives rain (vv. 19-22).
14.theology:
Creation suffers under human sin (vv. 4-6; Rom 8:20-22). Prayer that appeals to God's name rather than to human merit is the highest form of prayer (v. 7; Ps 79:9; Dan 9:18), yet God measures prayers against the direction of a life: he answers the feet, not the eloquence (v. 10).

Worship used as a lever while the course is unchanged is refused (vv. 11-12; Isa 1:15). False prophecy is the deceit of the preacher's own mind (v. 14), teachers are judged by the standard they preached (v. 15), and hearers are not acquitted for having been deceived (v. 16; 5:31).

God commands tears over judgment (v. 17). A perfect prayer is not the same as repentance (vv. 19-22 with 15:1), and the mercy that outlasts this refusal is stated by the same prophet in Lam 3:22-23.
14.examples:
Empty jars carried back from the cisterns, in the book that called sin a broken cistern.

Nobles' servants and farmers making the same gesture, covering their heads.

A doe walking away from her newborn because there is no grass.

God described as a tourist who stops for the night.

Preaching what you find plausible and calling it the word of the LORD.

A prayer that would score full marks, and feet that have not changed direction.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to me, "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people. Send them out of my sight, and let them go!<sup>2</sup>And when they ask you, 'Where shall we go?' you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: "'Those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword; those who are for famine, to famine, and those who are for captivity, to captivity.'<sup>3</sup>I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to tear, and the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.<sup>4</sup>And I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, did in Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>"Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem, or who will grieve for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare?<sup>6</sup>You have rejected me, declares the LORD; you keep going backward, so I have stretched out my hand against you and destroyed you— I am weary of relenting.<sup>7</sup>I have winnowed them with a winnowing fork in the gates of the land; I have bereaved them; I have destroyed my people; they did not turn from their ways.<sup>8</sup>I have made their widows more in number than the sand of the seas; I have brought against the mothers of young men a destroyer at noonday; I have made anguish and terror fall upon them suddenly.<sup>9</sup>She who bore seven has grown feeble; she has fainted away; her sun went down while it was yet day; she has been shamed and disgraced. And the rest of them I will give to the sword before their enemies, declares the LORD."<sup>10</sup>Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and contention to the whole land! I have not lent, nor have I borrowed, yet all of them curse me.<sup>11</sup>The LORD said, "Have I not set you free for their good? Have I not pleaded for you before the enemy in the time of trouble and in the time of distress?<sup>12</sup>Can one break iron, iron from the north, and bronze?<sup>13</sup>"Your wealth and your treasures I will give as spoil, without price, for all your sins, throughout all your territory.<sup>14</sup>I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."<sup>15</sup>O LORD, you know; remember me and visit me, and take vengeance for me on my persecutors. In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach.<sup>16</sup>Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart, for I am called by your name, O LORD, God of hosts.<sup>17</sup>I did not sit in the company of revelers, nor did I rejoice; I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation.<sup>18</sup>Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?<sup>19</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD: "If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them.<sup>20</sup>And I will make you to this people a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail over you, for I am with you to save you and deliver you, declares the LORD.<sup>21</sup>I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Though Moses and Samuel Stood Before Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people (v. 1). Asked where they should go, they are sent to pestilence, sword, famine and captivity (v. 2), with four destroyers appointed (v. 3), all because of what Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, did in Jerusalem (v. 4). Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem? (v. 5). They kept going backward, and God says, I am weary of relenting (v. 6); he has winnowed and bereaved them (vv. 7-8), and she who bore seven has fainted away, her sun went down while it was yet day (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The greatest intercessors in Israel's history could not turn this, and the sins of a king two generations back are still working themselves out.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to me, "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people. Send them out of my sight, and let them go! And when they ask you, 'Where shall we go?' you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: "'Those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword; those who are for famine, to famine, and those who are for captivity, to captivity.' I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to tear, and the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy. And I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, did in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the LORD said to me, "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people. Send them out of my sight, and let them go!

This is the answer to the faultless prayer at the end of chapter 14, and it is devastating.

Moses and Samuel are named because they are the two men in Israel's story who most famously changed God's mind by praying. Moses stood in the breach at Sinai when the nation deserved destruction, and the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people (Exod 32:14). Samuel said it would be a sin against God for him to stop praying for Israel (1 Sam 12:23). The psalm remembers both: They called to the LORD, and he answered them (Ps 99:6).

God says that if those two were standing here making that case, his heart would not turn. It is the strongest way of saying that the moment for this generation has passed, and it explains why Jeremiah has three times been forbidden to pray.

And when they ask you, 'Where shall we go?' you shall say to them, 'Thus says the LORD: "'Those who are for pestilence, to pestilence, and those who are for the sword, to the sword; those who are for famine, to famine, and those who are for captivity, to captivity.'

They will ask the practical question people always ask in a crisis: where do we go? The answer is a grim allocation list. Not a refuge, but a destination each.

I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to tear, and the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.

Sword, dogs, birds, beasts: the sequence of a battlefield after the fighting stops. It is deliberately without dignity, because that is what the end of a siege looks like.

And I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth because of what Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, did in Jerusalem.

Manasseh had been dead for decades. He reigned fifty-five years, filled Jerusalem with idols and innocent blood, and — the books of Kings and Chronicles agree — repented late in his own life. His personal forgiveness did not undo what he had built into the nation.

Face that honestly. Sin can be forgiven and still leave consequences running through families and institutions for generations. The father who is restored to God may still watch his children live with what his years of neglect made normal. Grace is free; it is not a time machine.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem, or who will grieve for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare? You have rejected me, declares the LORD; you keep going backward, so I have stretched out my hand against you and destroyed you— I am weary of relenting. I have winnowed them with a winnowing fork in the gates of the land; I have bereaved them; I have destroyed my people; they did not turn from their ways. I have made their widows more in number than the sand of the seas; I have brought against the mothers of young men a destroyer at noonday; I have made anguish and terror fall upon them suddenly. She who bore seven has grown feeble; she has fainted away; her sun went down while it was yet day; she has been shamed and disgraced. And the rest of them I will give to the sword before their enemies, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Who will have pity on you, O Jerusalem, or who will grieve for you? Who will turn aside to ask about your welfare?

Three questions, and they are about loneliness rather than punishment. Who will feel sorry? Who will mourn? Who will even stop to ask how you are? A city that made itself a byword will find the neighbours passing on the other side.

You have rejected me, declares the LORD; you keep going backward, so I have stretched out my hand against you and destroyed you— I am weary of relenting.

You keep going backward — the same charge as 7:24. And then a phrase to stop at: I am weary of relenting.

Relenting is what God has been doing for centuries. Every warning not carried out, every disaster postponed, every prophet sent instead of an army was God relenting. He is not saying that mercy has run out in principle — three chapters later he will say that if a nation turns he will relent of the disaster he intended (18:8). He is saying that this generation has used his patience as a policy.

I have winnowed them with a winnowing fork in the gates of the land; I have bereaved them; I have destroyed my people; they did not turn from their ways.

Four first-person verbs, and the third is I have destroyed my people. God does not distance himself from what is happening, and he does not stop calling them his.

The reason is stated last, plainly: they did not turn from their ways. Everything in this book comes back to that sentence.

I have made their widows more in number than the sand of the seas; I have brought against the mothers of young men a destroyer at noonday; I have made anguish and terror fall upon them suddenly. She who bore seven has grown feeble; she has fainted away; her sun went down while it was yet day; she has been shamed and disgraced. And the rest of them I will give to the sword before their enemies, declares the LORD."

The promise to Abraham was descendants like the sand of the sea; now the widows are counted that way. Seven sons was the picture of a blessed mother, and this one has lost them all: her sun went down while it was yet day.

That phrase has comforted and haunted the bereaved ever since, because it names the particular cruelty of losing a child. The light going at noon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — A Man of Strife and Contention
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and contention to the whole land! — though he has neither lent nor borrowed, everyone curses him (v. 10). God replies that he has set him free for their good and pleaded for him in trouble (v. 11), and asks whether iron from the north can be broken (v. 12). Judah's wealth will be spoil (v. 13), and they will serve their enemies in a land they do not know (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet wishes he had never been born, and God answers him without apology and without contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and contention to the whole land! I have not lent, nor have I borrowed, yet all of them curse me. The LORD said, "Have I not set you free for their good? Have I not pleaded for you before the enemy in the time of trouble and in the time of distress?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and contention to the whole land! I have not lent, nor have I borrowed, yet all of them curse me.

Now the prophet breaks, and this is the third of his confessions. He turns to the woman who gave him birth and wishes she had not. Job said it in his ashes: Let the day perish on which I was born (Job 3:3).

What he cannot bear is what he has become: a man of strife and contention to the whole land. He never wanted to be a controversialist. He is a village priest's son who would have been content to be ignored, and he is the most argued-about man in the country.

The detail about lending is the saddest touch. Debt was the usual reason for a man to be hated in a small society. I have not lent, nor have I borrowed — he has given nobody any of the ordinary grounds for a grudge, and they curse him anyway. He is hated purely for the message.

Anyone who has been disliked for their faith rather than for their faults will understand the particular loneliness of this verse.

The LORD said, "Have I not set you free for their good? Have I not pleaded for you before the enemy in the time of trouble and in the time of distress?

The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew here is uncertain, and translations differ. What comes through is that God answers, and that his answer is about his own care: he has been at work for Jeremiah's good and has pleaded for him when enemies pressed.

Notice what God does not do. He does not rebuke the outburst, and he does not pretend the pain is unreasonable. He replies.

verseByVerse.quote: Can one break iron, iron from the north, and bronze? "Your wealth and your treasures I will give as spoil, without price, for all your sins, throughout all your territory. I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can one break iron, iron from the north, and bronze?

A question about metallurgy that is really about politics. The iron from the north is Babylon, and nobody breaks it — certainly not Judah's foreign policy. It is the answer to every plan for escape that the palace has been making.

"Your wealth and your treasures I will give as spoil, without price, for all your sins, throughout all your territory.

Without price: no ransom, no tribute paid to buy it back, no compensation. The treasures simply change hands. A nation that trusted its reserves discovers they were never security.

I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, for in my anger a fire is kindled that shall burn forever."

The sentence of 5:19 again, and the point of it is precision: you served foreign gods at home, so you will serve foreigners abroad. Exile is not random misfortune; it is the sin made visible and lived in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Your Words Were Found, and I Ate Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O LORD, you know; remember me and visit me, and know that for your sake I bear reproach (v. 15). Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart (v. 16). He sat alone rather than with the revellers, because God's hand was on him (v. 17). Then the accusation: Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail? (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The same words that were his joy have cost him every friendship, and he tells God that he feels like a dry streambed.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you know; remember me and visit me, and take vengeance for me on my persecutors. In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach. Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart, for I am called by your name, O LORD, God of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD, you know; remember me and visit me, and take vengeance for me on my persecutors. In your forbearance take me not away; know that for your sake I bear reproach.

He prays, and the first words are the ones every sufferer needs: O LORD, you know. Not, explain it; you know.

Then a request that shows how well he understands his own situation. God is being patient with his persecutors — and that patience is the very thing endangering the prophet. In your forbearance take me not away: do not let me be killed while you are being slow to judge them. It is a real prayer from inside a real danger.

And the ground of the appeal: for your sake I bear reproach. That is the phrase the New Testament picks up for everyone who suffers for Christ, and it is the only thing that makes the suffering bearable.

Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart, for I am called by your name, O LORD, God of hosts.

Here is one of the loveliest sentences in the Bible about Scripture, and it comes from a man in the middle of a breakdown.

Your words were found — perhaps a memory of the scroll discovered in the temple in Josiah's reign, perhaps simply the moment God's word came to him. And I ate them: not admired, studied or filed. Eaten, taken in as food, made part of himself. Ezekiel was given a scroll to eat and found it as sweet as honey (Ezek 3:3). The psalmist said, How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! (Ps 119:103). Jesus answered the tempter, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matt 4:4).

And the result: a joy and the delight of my heart. This is the man who has just wished he had never been born. Both are true at once, and anyone who has walked with God through a hard season knows that they can be.

verseByVerse.quote: I did not sit in the company of revelers, nor did I rejoice; I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation. Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I did not sit in the company of revelers, nor did I rejoice; I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation.

Here is the cost of the previous verse. The word that was his joy has taken away his company. He did not join the parties — partly because he could not bring himself to, partly because a man who says what he says is not invited twice.

I sat alone, because your hand was upon me. The hand of God is usually spoken of as protection or power. Here it is what keeps a man out of the room. Faithfulness is often isolating, and Jeremiah does not pretend it is noble or that he enjoys it. He is lonely and he blames God for it, accurately.

Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?

This is the sharpest thing Jeremiah ever says, and it should be read slowly. In a dry country a wadi runs full in the rains and is a bed of stones in the summer. Travellers died going to one on the strength of a memory.

He is saying to God: I think you might be a stream that dries up. And the accusation lands exactly where this book began — God had called himself the fountain of living waters and the people's idols the broken cisterns (2:13). Now the prophet who preached that sermon asks whether the fountain is seasonal.

Notice what Scripture does with this. It writes it down and keeps it. The Bible is not embarrassed by a servant of God accusing God of unreliability, because the God of the Bible is not fragile, and because believers need to know that somebody in the book has felt what they are feeling.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–21 — If You Return, I Will Restore You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them (v. 19). And the promise of the call is renewed: I will make you to this people a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail over you, for I am with you to save you and deliver you (v. 20), delivered out of the hand of the wicked (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: God calls his own prophet to repent, and then gives him back his commission with the original promise attached.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD: "If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them. And I will make you to this people a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail over you, for I am with you to save you and deliver you, declares the LORD. I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the LORD: "If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them.

God's answer is not what a modern reader expects, and it is exactly right. He does not comfort first. He calls his prophet to repent.

If you return, I will restore you — the same word Jeremiah has been preaching to the nation is now addressed to him. His complaint went past lament into accusation, and God treats him as an adult: turn, and you will be restored to your place, standing before me as a servant stands before a king.

If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth. He is to sort his speech. Self-pity and bitterness are worthless; God's word is precious; and the promise attached is staggering — you shall be as my mouth.

Then the rule for every minister since: They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them. The pressure of an audience is constant, and the temptation is to be shaped by the people you are speaking to until you are saying what they would have said anyway. That is how the false prophets of chapter 14 were made. The direction of influence must run one way.

And I will make you to this people a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail over you, for I am with you to save you and deliver you, declares the LORD. I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless."

And God gives him back his call, in the words of the first chapter (1:18-19). A bronze wall; opposition that does not prevail; I am with you.

Two things stand out. The promise is repeated rather than improved, because it was always sufficient and the man had simply lost sight of it. And it is given after the rebuke, not instead of it. God's way with his exhausted servants is neither to ignore their sin nor to withdraw his promise, but to call them back and then hand them the same commission again.

Jeremiah went back to work for another thirty years.

15.title: A Deceitful Brook, and the Bronze Wall
15.overview:
God answers the faultless prayer of chapter 14: even if Moses and Samuel stood before him, his heart would not turn toward this people (v. 1). They are allotted to pestilence, sword, famine and captivity, with four destroyers appointed, because of what Manasseh did in Jerusalem (vv. 2-4). No one will pity Jerusalem; they keep going backward, and God is weary of relenting; widows outnumber the sand, and the mother of seven faints as her sun goes down at noon (vv. 5-9).

Jeremiah wishes he had never been born: a man of strife whom everyone curses though he has neither lent nor borrowed (v. 10). God replies that he has worked for his good and pleaded for him (v. 11), and declares that iron from the north cannot be broken, that Judah's treasures will be spoil, and that they will serve enemies in an unknown land (vv. 12-14).

The prophet prays: you know; remember me; for your sake I bear reproach (v. 15). God's words were found and he ate them, and they were the delight of his heart (v. 16), yet they left him sitting alone (v. 17), and he asks whether God will be to him like a brook that fails (v. 18). God calls him to return, to speak what is precious and not what is worthless, never to be shaped by his hearers, and renews the promise of the bronze wall and of deliverance (vv. 19-21).
15.theology:
Intercession has limits: there is a point at which even the greatest intercessors would not turn God's heart (v. 1; Exod 32:14; 1 Sam 12:23). Forgiven sin can still leave consequences running for generations (v. 4). God's long patience is real and can be presumed upon (v. 6; compare 18:8).

God's word is food and delight to those who receive it (v. 16; Ezek 3:3; Ps 119:103; Matt 4:4), and it can isolate the one who carries it (v. 17). Scripture preserves a prophet's accusation that God may be a brook that fails (v. 18), because faith may speak honestly to God.

God calls his own servants to repent when complaint hardens into accusation, then restores them and renews the original commission (vv. 19-21; 1:18-19). A minister must be shaped by God's word rather than by his hearers (v. 19).
15.examples:
The two men who most famously changed God's mind, named as unable to change it now.

A king forgiven late, whose work in the nation outlived him.

The light going at noon for a mother who has lost her children.

Hated with none of the usual grounds for a grudge.

Eating the word, and losing every invitation because of it.

A wadi full in the rains and a bed of stones in summer.
